activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues' 1993 study of violinists described 'deliberate practice': effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours.
story:
Alyssa taped the whiteboard to the rink boards where the U14 girls could see it, then untaped it because the diagram looked like a ransom note. Behind her, twelve twelve-year-olds were already firing pucks at the empty net, the way they did every practice, and by the end of every practice they would still be terrible at passing. She knew this because she had watched them for three weeks. They could skate. They could shoot. The moment a pass had to travel more than six feet, it ended up in someone's skates or against the glass, and they laughed, and the game went on.

"They only want to scrimmage," her cousin Dev had told her when she took the volunteer job. Dev ran the association like a small technocracy, ice time allocated by spreadsheet, and he had been peevish about giving her the Tuesday hour until she promised to submit practice plans in advance. "You get fifty minutes. Don't waste it on drills they'll malign behind your back."

She had written the first plan at her kitchen table with a psych textbook open beside her, left over from the community college course she'd started in the spring. She'd skimmed it for coaching and found a study instead: violinists at a music academy, 1993, K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues. The best players hadn't logged the most hours overall; what separated them was what the researchers called deliberate practice, effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, instead of just accumulating time. Alyssa had read the paragraph twice, then gone to the window. Her own hockey career had ended at sixteen with nothing to show for eleven years of ice except smooth crossovers and a wrist shot she could still land in her sleep. Hours. She had logged so many hours.

Flashback first, though, before the plan could exist: Alyssa at fourteen, sitting on the bench during a tournament in Pembroke while her coach drew up a power play on his clipboard. He had never once told her what she was bad at. He'd told her she was doing great, that she was a gamer, that she brought energy, and she had believed him right up until the rep team cuts came out and her name wasn't on the list. Her mother had said maybe it was politics. Alyssa had known better even then, and had never asked anyone to tell her the truth, which was its own kind of politics.

So on Tuesday she blew the whistle inside the first two minutes. Pucks went in the bucket. The girls groaned, one of them, Priya, loudly and with feeling.

"We're not scrimmaging today."

"Why not."

"Because we scrimmage every day and you still can't pass."

"We can pass."

"Show me. Ten feet, tape to tape, ten in a row." They got to four before Shauna put one into the corner, and everyone looked at the ceiling of the arena as though it might intervene.

Alyssa set up the drill she'd designed at the kitchen table: two lines, one passer, one receiver skating across the slot, pass had to lead the skater, and every miss meant the passer had to call out what she'd done wrong before she could rotate. Shauna's first five attempts went wide or behind. "I don't know," she said, the sixth time. "Tell me where it went," Alyssa said. "My feet?" "So fix it." On the eighth, Shauna pulled up mid-release, set her hips, and the puck arrived on Priya's tape as she crossed the far post. Priya didn't even break stride. Nobody said anything, but the next girl in line skated harder to her spot, and Alyssa wrote something on the whiteboard in block letters: WEAK PASSING UNDER MOVEMENT. 8 MISSES BEFORE 1 CLEAN. It wasn't a lesson, it was a number, and the girls kept glancing at it.

The number moved. Eleven attempts, then seven, then, near the end of the hour, a string of six clean in a row before the Zamboni light came on and Dev appeared at the gate with his clipboard.

"Fifty minutes, no scrimmage. The parents are going to malign me in the parking lot."

"It's called deliberate practice," Alyssa said. "It works on the thing you're worst at. That's the whole point."

Dev watched Priya take a pass in full stride and bury it, top corner, no celebration, just a hard loop back to the line. He wrote something on his clipboard.

"Same plan Thursday?"

"Same drill. Harder."

He nodded and let the gate clang shut behind him. The girls were already whacking pucks toward the bucket themselves, without being asked, and Alyssa stood at the whiteboard and drew a small box beside the number six, left it empty, and capped the marker.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Code-switching is moving between two languages within one conversation; it is common among fluent bilinguals and is not by itself a sign of weak skill.
story:
The debate topic was printed on the whiteboard in Señora Vega's tidy, vestigial cursive, a style nobody under forty used anymore: "Should the school day begin at ten instead of eight?" Under it, the rule that had Sara's stomach folding in on itself like a paper crane: five minutes, entirely in Spanish, no English, or the team lost a full letter grade.

"Entirely," her partner, Danny, whispered as they huddled over a single shared desk in the back corner of room 214. The room smelled of dry-erase marker and the oranges Señora Vega kept in a bowl like some ascetic offering, never eaten, just displayed. "Even the part where I panic? What do I do, panic in Spanish?"

"You say 'no sé' with conviction," Sara said. "People respect conviction."

Danny was fluent by accident; his grandmother lived with his family and Spanish came out of him the way breathing did. Sara had gotten to this class by working, flashcard by flashcard, Saturday mornings sacrificed to verb conjugations the way other people sacrificed them to sleep. She wanted the five minutes because the university admissions packet had a line about demonstrated proficiency, but also, though she would not have said this out loud, because she wanted to hold the language in her hands without feeling it slip.

At lunch they practiced in the cafeteria, which smelled of industrial pizza and floor wax. Sara got through ninety seconds on adolescent sleep research before disaster: "Los estudiantes need, uh, los estudiantes necesitan more sleep, because their brains are still, uh, developing, which is why the schedule should change." She heard the English words land like dropped trays. Danny winced. Sara put her forehead on the table next to her milk carton.

"I did it again," she said into the laminate.

"You do it every time you get nervous," Danny said. He peeled his orange, though it was Señora Vega's kind of orange, small and sour. "You know it's not a failure thing, right? There's a word for it. Code-switching. Moving between two languages in one conversation. My abuela does it constantly and nobody would call her weak in either language. It's common among people who are actually fluent."

Sara lifted her head. "I'm not fluent."

"You're close enough that your brain treats English like a door it can walk through," Danny said. "That's the thing. It's common among fluent bilinguals. It doesn't mean what you think it means."

She turned this over through sixth period chemistry, writing LA CLAVE at the top of her notes and then, feeling dramatic, crossing it out. What Danny was describing was not the opposite of skill. It was almost a symptom of it. Which meant the rule, entirely in Spanish, was asking her not to erase a weakness but to close a door on purpose, for five minutes, that fluent people left swinging. She could not decide whether that made the rule stupid or whether it was exactly the discipline she needed, and she liked even less that both could be true at once. She decided to hold the question instead of answering it, the way you hold a hot cup, testing.

Fourth period the next day, the desks were pushed into two facing rows. Señora Vega sat by the window with a stopwatch and a clipboard, sunlight moving across her bracelets. Danny went first, sailed, floated, occasionally seemed to forget he was being graded. Then it was Sara's turn, and Marcus from the opposing side folded his arms like a lawyer in a show about lawyers.

She started. The Spanish came, a little slow, then faster. "Los estudiantes adolescentes necesitan dormir más porque sus cerebros siguen desarrollándose. Si la escuela comenzara a las diez..." Marcus interrupted with a question about parents' work schedules and her mind went white, and the English came up her throat like water.

"Because, because the parents would, los padres tendrían que..." She stopped. Somewhere a pencil tapped. Marcus smirked, the specific smirk of someone winning on a technicality rather than an argument. Sara put her hand flat on the desk, felt the cool press of laminate, and thought: this is a door, and I am allowed to close it.

"Repito," she said, slowly, and each word after that was chosen like a coin from the bottom of a purse. "Los padres tendrían dificultades, sí, pero las dificultades existen en ambos casos. La pregunta no es si hay dificultades. La pregunta es cuáles podemos soportar." She heard the room go quiet in a different way, not bored-quiet but listening-quiet. When the stopwatch beeped she had thirty seconds left and a full argument on the board of her mind, unspent.

Afterward, in the hall, Danny found her at the water fountain. "You switched twice," he said. "Once to English, once from it. Second one was the impressive one."

"Which one counts?" Sara said.

He shrugged and tossed her the sour orange he had smuggled out of 214. "Depends who's keeping score."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 1 hypertension means a systolic reading of 130 to 139 or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89.
story:
Amelia had signed up to be a peer health educator because the poster said "Make a difference," and because Tuesday afternoons were otherwise dedicated to her grandmother's querulous commentary on the price of groceries, delivered over the phone like war dispatches. The training was held in the health center's back room, where a skeleton named Yorick wore a paper party hat someone had left in September. Today they were supposed to practice explaining consent, contraception, and where to get tested for infections, and Amelia's turn was next.

The trouble was her practice partner, Dex, who had appointed himself the world's most difficult hypothetical teenager. "Okay," he said, settling into his chair like a lawyer about to bill her. "Say I don't want to use anything. Say I say my last partner said it was fine."

"Then I'd say consent has to be yours to give," Amelia said. "It's not transferable. Like a bus pass." She had been drilling the phrases all week: consent is ongoing, it's specific, it can be withdrawn, silence isn't agreement. Saying them out loud to Dex's smug hypothetical face was different from whispering them to her ceiling. "You can say yes to one thing and no to another, and you can change your mind halfway through, and the other person has to actually check, not just assume."

"And contraception?"

"Options, not lectures." She laid out the pamphlets like tarot cards. "Condoms, the pill, the implant, the IUD. Different people, different tradeoffs. If someone asks about the implant I can tell them it goes in the arm and lasts years, and that the health center here does it, and that the cost can be amortized over that whole time so it stops sounding scary." Dex nodded slowly, as if conceding a point in chess.

He was reaching for his final weapon, the "where do I even get tested" gambit, when Amelia's phone buzzed. A photo from her grandmother: a page from Grandpa Walt's home blood pressure log, numbers marching down the margin in his small square handwriting. 134 over 86. Then 132 over 84. Then, from this morning, 138 over 82.

She stared at it. Last weekend at their house she had flipped through the log herself, half listening to Grandpa Walt insisting the machine squeezed too hard and made everything worse, clearly the machine's fault, a medical machination designed to frighten old men into clinics. She'd taken a health elective where the 2017 American guideline had come up, and she remembered enough to be uneasy. Under that guideline, stage 1 hypertension meant a systolic reading of 130 to 139, or a diastolic of 80 to 89. She said it to herself twice to fix it in place. Grandpa Walt's numbers sat squarely inside both ranges, every single day of the log.

"You look like you saw a ghost," Dex said.

"Stage 1 hypertension," she said, mostly to the phone. "That's what it's called. His numbers are all in it. Like, all of them."

"Is that bad?"

"I don't know if it's bad." That was the honest part, the part she kept circling. "The guideline is a cutoff, not a diagnosis. I know the numbers qualify him for the name. I don't know what happens next, and I'm not going to pretend I do." She typed to her grandmother: can you ask him to show the log to Dr. Okafor? Not an alarm. Just an appointment. Then, after a pause: I'll come with him if he wants. Her grandmother replied with three thumbs-up and a picture of a pie, which was her dialect for "understood, also there is pie."

Their supervisor, Ms. Reyes, leaned over from the sign-in table. "Everything alright?"

"Family math," Amelia said. "Doing the subtraction." Ms. Reyes, who had long ago stopped being surprised by anything in the back room, gave her the pamphlet stack for the front desk and moved on.

"Okay, final question," Dex said, cracking his knuckles with theatrical menace. "Say I'm nervous about getting tested. Say I'd rather not know."

Amelia thought of Grandpa Walt, who would also rather not know, who would rather blame the machine, and who was going to be driven to Dr. Okafor's office by a granddaughter armed with a pie. "Then I'd say I get it," she said. "But knowing is a thing you can act on, and not knowing is just waiting with worse imagination. Also it's fifteen minutes and they'll let you pick the music."

"Bold claim."

"Ms. Reyes told me. There's a playlist." She squared the pamphlets and stood up. "Now if you'll excuse me, I have to go negotiate with an old man about a doctor's appointment, and I'm bringing reinforcements." She held up her phone, the pie picture glowing on the screen, and Dex saluted her with Yorick's paper hat.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: In the Jewish Passover tradition, the festive meal is called a Seder, a Hebrew word meaning 'order', because its rituals follow a fixed sequence from start to finish.
story:
Benjamin had agreed to lead the Seder in February, when it still felt like a distant, abstract favor, and now it was April and the kitchen smelled of brisket and his grandmother's florid handwriting was spread across the table in front of him, three pages of instructions that contradicted each other by page two. His grandfather, who had led the meal for forty years, was in the study with the door half open, not helping, which Benjamin understood was its own kind of statement.

"You're putting the Seder plate on the wrong end," his cousin Dara said, leaning over his shoulder. She was fourteen and enjoyed being right more than she enjoyed anything else at family gatherings.

"It goes where Zayde puts it."

"Zayde puts it near the head. You're at the head now. So it goes near you." She slid the plate down the tablecloth, the shank bone catching the light, and Benjamin let her. It was easier than arguing, and anyway he had a different problem: the sequence. Kadesh, then what. Urchatz. Then what came after Urchatz. He had studied the haggadah on the train down, folding over page corners, and on the train the order had seemed obvious, a river flowing in one direction. At the table, with fourteen relatives arriving in forty minutes, the river kept forking.

Their rabbi had said something in his office a week earlier that Benjamin had written in his phone and read eleven times since. He had gone to ask which blessing went with the second cup of wine, and instead of answering directly the rabbi had said, "You know the meal is called a Seder because the word means order. The whole night follows a fixed sequence, start to finish." Then he'd smiled in a way that suggested this was either a comfort or a warning, and told Benjamin the second cup came before the meal, and let him go. Benjamin had walked home thinking that "order" was a strange name for a night built around a story of chaos and wandering, forty years of desert between two orderly cups of wine.

His mother found him in the hallway, still holding the haggadah like a shield. "Relax," she said. "You've been coming to this table since you were born. Your body knows more than your notes do." That was her whole philosophy, more or less. She'd married into the family and still, after nineteen years, poured the second cup at the wrong time every other year, laughing, saying the wine didn't mind. Benjamin loved that about her and also it terrified him, because Zayde did mind, quietly, and this year Zayde was watching from the study with the door half open, and if Benjamin poured the wrong cup at the wrong time he would see it as proof of something.

The guests came in a flood of coats and casserole dishes. His aunt Rivka kissed him on both cheeks and said, "So you're the leader now," and the word leader sat strangely on him, like a jacket cut for a bigger man. He took his seat. Fourteen faces, some patient, some hungry, all waiting, and Dara gave him a small nod that meant she had decided to be on his side, at least publicly.

"Kadesh," he began, and lifted the first cup.

The early steps went well enough, the way the first mile of a race always does. Then his uncle started a story about a Seder in Buenos Aires in 1987, a genuinely good story, and while everyone laughed Benjamin felt the next step slide out of his grip, and he sat there with his hand flat on the page, transfix, everyone's eyes on him, waiting. Two voices in him at once: his mother's voice saying the story is the point, and his grandfather's voice saying the order is the point, and no voice at all saying which was right.

Then he found the page corner he'd folded, and the folded corner was enough. "Urchatz," he said, and they washed, and later he found the next corner, and the next, and somewhere around the matzah he stopped needing the corners because the sequence began to carry him instead of the other way around. He understood, mid-sentence during the Four Questions, which Dara's little brother stumbled through with the flat, doomed courage of a boy who has practiced, that his mother and his grandfather had been describing the same night from two sides. The order was not a cage; it was the shape the story poured itself into so that it could hold everyone at once, the quick and the slow, the believers and the ones there for the brisket. Or maybe that was too generous. He honestly could not tell yet whether he had reconciled anything or only survived it.

When they reached the meal itself, the talking and passing and reaching, Zayde came out of the study at last and sat down across from him. He looked at the Seder plate, correctly placed, and at the four cups lined up, two empty, two full, in their proper futures. He picked up his fork, paused, and said, "After the meal, it's Tzafun. The hidden piece. You remember where it's hidden?" and Benjamin nodded, though he did not, and started eating fast so his grandfather wouldn't ask twice.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers popularized the '10,000-hour rule', though Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours.
story:
The door of the studio had a brass knocker shaped like a treble clef, which Henry thought was trying too hard. He had been taking cello lessons for six weeks, and every Thursday he arrived early and sat on the bench in the hallway, listening through the wall to the lesson before his, a girl working through some Brahms he couldn't name yet. His teacher, Ms. Ansel, believed in starting from sound rather than symbols, so for the first month he had only listened and hummed before she let him touch the instrument at all.

The trouble started with Dev, his best friend since seventh grade, who had come over on Tuesday with a bag of chips and an opinion. "You know it's pointless, right," Dev had said, feet on Henry's desk chair. "Gladwell's book, Outliers, 2008. The ten-thousand-hour rule. You're sixteen. You'd be like thirty before you were any good." Dev was reading economics blogs lately, having decided that stagflation was the most interesting thing that had ever happened to a country, and he delivered facts the way other people delivered insults, with relish and no malice.

"That's not what it says," Henry had said, though honestly he had only heard about the book secondhand, the way everyone had, the number floating around school like a rumor with a footnote. Ten thousand hours. He'd done the arithmetic in his head that night, lying awake, estimating: two hours a day, five years, or one hour a day for ten. Either way the number was a wall, and he was standing at the bottom of it holding a practice mute.

He had meant to ask Ms. Ansel directly, but Thursday came and she was in one of her moods where the metronome did all the talking. He was working on a shift from first to fourth position, and his hand kept arriving late and heavy, like a guest who hadn't recuperated from the trip before knocking. "Again," she said, and tapped, and he did it again, and again it was late. On the fifth try something happened that he couldn't have described: his elbow moved first, and the hand simply arrived where it needed to be, and the note bloomed instead of landing.

"There," she said, and stopped the metronome. "Do you know what you just did?"

"I got lucky."

"You let the wrong thing lead. You've been sending your fingers first, like they're the ones with the map." She wrote something in her notebook, which he'd never been allowed to see. "That took you forty minutes. Some people take a month, practicing an hour a day. Some take a week."

That night he did what he should have done weeks ago and looked it up himself, Dev's chips still half-finished on the desk. It took four searches before he found the actual claim and then the part after it: Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers had popularized the ten-thousand-hour rule, but Ericsson, whose research it came from, had later said that the quality of practice mattered more than any fixed number of hours. Henry read it twice, then a third time, feeling something between vindication and vertigo. The number wasn't a lie exactly, but it wasn't the whole thing either, the way a recipe that only listed cooking time and no ingredients wasn't quite a recipe.

He texted Dev a screenshot, then deleted the caption he'd drafted, which said told you, because it wasn't quite that simple either. Dev texted back a single word, "fair," and then, "still gonna be old though." Henry laughed at that alone in his room, which he recognized was the lowest form of laughter, but he took it.

The thing he couldn't resolve, walking to the bus stop with his cello case cutting into his shoulder, was what to do with both halves of it. Ten thousand hours was real enough as an idea, a way of saying that mastery was far away and not negotiable, and pretending otherwise was how people quit in month three. But quality was real too; his forty minutes that afternoon had moved him further than a week of noodling. Neither cancelled the other. He was left holding a number too big to think about comfortably and a principle too vague to hold onto, and the honest position, as far as he could find one, was that he'd practice like the quality mattered and accept that the hours would count themselves or not.

The putative ceiling, Dev would call it later, arguing over the school cafeteria's rectangular pizza, and Henry would let him have the word because it was a good one. "A putative ceiling," Dev said, pointing a fork at him, "can still be a real ceiling."

"Sure," Henry said. "But you're still thinking about economics and I'm thinking about my elbow."

On Thursday he got to the studio early again and sat on the bench, and through the wall the girl before him had moved on to something slower, a single held note that wavered and then steadied. He put his hands together on his knee, elbow out, fingers loose, and waited for the treble clef knocker to sound.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: GIS layers stored in different coordinate reference systems will not line up correctly until one is reprojected to match the other.
story:
The departures board kept flickering DELAYED beside the 6:40 to Porto, so Alexandre found a seat near the window wall, unfolded his mother's old laptop on his knees, and opened the project he was supposed to finish before Monday. Around him the terminal settled into its nighttime register: a janitor pushing a wide mop between the rows of bolted chairs, a sullen teenager two seats down with his hood up and his earbuds in, a family sleeping under airplane blankets as though the airport were a campsite they had chosen.

The project belonged to the summer course his geography teacher had pressed on him, a practicum in something called a geographic information system, which his teacher described as maps stacked like transparent sheets on a light table. Layer one was flood risk for the city of Coimbra, shaded in bands of blue. Layer two was housing stock, each block a small polygon. The assignment was to overlay them and name the neighbourhoods where the two layers agreed, where people lived on ground the water claimed.

Alexandre had grown up in one of those neighbourhoods, if the maps were right about it. The spring he was eleven, the Mondego had come up through the storm drains and taken the ground-floor flat where he and his mother lived, and afterward she had moved them uphill to a fourth-floor walkup above a hardware store, and she had said, at the time and often after, that they would never live on low ground again. He had chosen Coimbra on purpose. He wanted to see the flood map disagree with her, or agree with her, and he was honest enough with himself not to know which result he was hoping for.

He loaded the two layers and set them both visible. The housing polygons appeared where he expected, a dense grid on the flat eastern bank. Then the river arrived, and it arrived wrong. The blue channel of the Mondego cut straight through the middle of the city hall, a building Alexandre had stood in front of, a building that was on dry pavement a full kilometre from any water. He zoomed out, sure he had panned something sideways, but the river only lay there, patient and impossible, crossing the market square, forking around the university library.

"You look like a man watching a crime," said a voice. The woman in the next seat had a boarding pass for Lisbon tucked under her coffee cup and the particular posture of someone who flew twice a week and had stopped finding it interesting. She nodded at his screen. "That's a river in a strange place."

"It's in the middle of the city hall," Alexandre said. "I've been inside that building. There's no river in it."

She leaned over, and the screen's light caught her glasses. "I build these systems," she said. "For a utility company. And I will give you one hint and nothing else, because my son is your age and he learns nothing when I lecture." She tapped the corner of the screen, where the layers' properties sat in small grey text. "Look at what each layer says about its coordinate reference system. Compare them. That's the whole hint."

He opened the properties. The housing layer named one coordinate reference system; the flood layer named another, its coordinates recorded in a different way altogether. He sat with that for a moment, watching the maintenance trucks out on the tarmac, their beacon lights sweeping the wet asphalt. The layers were both describing the same city, the same ground, but each was describing it in its own terms, and the software had simply believed both of them at once and drawn the consequences. He found a tool in the menu, the word reproject sitting beside it, and applied it to the flood layer, telling it to match the housing layer's system.

The river moved. It slid half a kilometre north and settled into its true channel, and the whole map reorganised itself around that correction, the way a sentence changes when you finally hear which word was misplaced. And now the overlay told him something. The flood band reached across the eastern bank and covered, almost exactly, the grid of streets where he had lived until he was eleven. His mother's old flat sat inside the deepest blue. But the band also covered two blocks uphill from it, solid nineteenth-century buildings his mother had always called safe, and it left dry a low riverside stretch near the market that she refused even to walk through. Her instincts were a map drawn from one flood, one spring, one year, and the flood risk layer was drawn from many, and the two did not agree, and he could not yet say which one to trust about the years to come.

The woman had gone back to her book, but she looked over when he sat forward. "It lines up now," he said.

"Then you're the one in a hundred who reads the metadata," she said. "My colleagues, and I say this with love, are pragmatists. They want the map finished by Friday." She stood, gathered her coat, and paused with her boarding pass in hand. "The honest ones footnote what they're not sure of. Remember that when you publish something."

Alexandre dragged the two layers on and off, one over the other, watching the blue band and the housing grid coincide and separate. Somewhere behind him his flight number was called, a voice too calm for the word final, and he closed the laptop without saving and stood, and put it in his backpack, and got in line.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Subtext is the meaning beneath what characters actually say, such as anger or love that a line never names out loud.
story:
Austin had wanted the directing slot since sophomore year, when he watched a senior move two chairs three feet apart and turn a dull argument into something unbearable to sit through. Now the slot was his, a one-act about two brothers fighting over their dead mother's record collection, and he stood in the black box theatre with a roll of spike tape and four actors who were all older than he was.

His first instinct was to plan everything. He spent a Sunday night drawing the stage on graph paper, plotting every crossing, every turn, so that by Monday's rehearsal he could hand out the blocking like a subpoena, each actor served with their required movements. Devon, who played the older brother, took one look at the diagram and laughed. "You want me to walk away on that line? That's the line where I finally admit I need him."

"But it looks good," Austin said. "The diagonal. It opens up the stage."

Devon looked at him for a long moment, then walked the diagonal anyway, nonchalant, hands in his pockets, and Austin saw immediately that it was wrong. The admission happened while the actor's body was already leaving. It looked like he didn't care. That night Austin sat with the graph paper and wondered how much of directing was geometry and how much was something the graph paper couldn't hold. Was a stage picture a picture of bodies, or a picture of what the bodies were hiding?

The next rehearsal, Priya, who played the younger brother's girlfriend, asked to try something. She'd rewritten her scene, the one where she tells the younger brother to stop idolizing his dead mother. In Priya's version, nobody said what they meant. The girlfriend talked about the weather in the car, about a parking ticket, about whether they should get food after, and the younger brother answered in the same flat coinage, and the scene ended with both of them still sitting there, saying nothing true.

"It's better this way," Priya said. "Nobody actually says it. In real life nobody says it."

"It's like subtext," Devon said, leaning against the record shelf. "The meaning underneath what they actually say. Anger, love, whatever. The line never names it out loud."

Austin had heard the word in English class, applied to Chekhov, and had filed it under things that belonged to essays. Now he watched Priya and Marcus run the rewritten scene and felt the floor of the play shift under him. When the girlfriend said, "There's a good burrito place on Fifth," her voice caught on the word good, and Marcus went still, and the whole audience-less room understood that she was asking him to stay, and that he understood, and that he would not answer. The graph paper could not have predicted the catch in her voice. Blocking was what you could plan. This was what you had to catch.

So he changed how he worked. Instead of announcing the moves, he asked questions. "Where do you want to be when you lie to him?" he asked Devon, and Devon thought about it, honestly thought, then walked to the record shelf and picked up an album and held it wrong, like a man who had never played a record in his life, holding his mother's thing as if it meant nothing. Austin's chest went tight. He burnedish nothing, arranged nothing; he just said, "Stay there," and wrote it down, and the note in his binder read only: holds it wrong on purpose?

He wasn't sure it would survive an audience. That was the part he couldn't test. Some of the quietest choices might read as nothing from twenty rows back, and some of the loud ones, the slammed doors and upturned chairs, might be the only things that landed. He thought about the senior from sophomore year, the two chairs moved three feet apart, and wondered whether she had known it would work or had simply believed it and been right. Maybe there was no way to know the difference beforehand. Maybe directing was making the bet anyway.

On Thursday his faculty advisor, Ms. Ro, watched a run-through from the back and afterward said only, "Tighter scene changes," and left, which Austin decided to take as a kind of victory.

Friday night, the small audience came. During Priya's burrito line, someone in the third row made a sound, half laugh, half something else. Austin stood at the tech table in the dark with his headset on, watching Devon hold the record wrong under a single blue light, and did not move his hands from the board. He didn't know yet if any of it had worked, only that the sound in the third row had been real, and Devon turned the album over slowly, and read the back of the sleeve, and said his next line to it rather than to Marcus.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Commencement means "beginning"; the word was used for graduation ceremonies because graduates begin a new status, such as being a bachelor or master.
story:
Charlotte found her father in the garage on the morning of graduation, hunched over the lawn mower with a socket wrench, though the lawn had already been cut twice that week. She stood in the doorway holding her cap, still flat in its packaging, and watched him loosen a bolt that did not need loosening.

"You're hiding," she said.

"I'm maintaining equipment." He set the wrench down and looked at her gown, which she had put on early because her mother wanted pictures before the heat arrived. "You could help me with this bolt."

She crouched beside him and held the nut steady while he turned. This was how they had always talked, side by side, hands busy, neither of them required to look at the other. He asked whether she had decided about the deferral yet, and she said no, and he said nothing, and she was grateful for the nothing.

The trouble was this: the university had offered her a place in the fall, and the wildlife center two towns over had offered her a paid internship for the same months, with housing above the raptor barn and a supervisor who had once let her transcribe a whole season of migration logs just because she asked. Her mother thought the internship was a detour dressed up as a calling. Her father thought whatever she thought, mostly, which was its own kind of pressure. Charlotte had spent two weeks making lists, and the lists had become two small saturnine piles on her desk, each one refusing to collapse into the other.

Her friend Priya arrived at noon with a garment steamer and a bag of bobby pins, having declared over text that Charlotte's household clearly could not be trusted with wrinkles. In the kitchen Priya steamed the gown while Charlotte's mother fanned the fabric with a cutting board, and for a while the room was just steam and laughter and the smell of the lemon cake cooling on the sill.

Charlotte said, mostly to the steam, "I keep feeling like it's a funeral for something."

"For what?"

"For being this. For this house, this kitchen. Everything I know how to be." She heard how it sounded and kept going anyway. "Four years and then it's over, and they hand you a hat."

Priya lifted the gown off the hanger and held it up to the window light, checking her work. "You know what the ceremony's actually called," she said. "Commencement. It means beginning. That's why they used the word, because you begin a new status. Like being a bachelor or a master." She shook out a crease at the hem. "So it's not a funeral. It's a launch, technically."

"Technically," Charlotte said, but something in her chest rearranged itself slightly, the way furniture moves when you finally stop dragging it sideways.

At the school, under a sun that made the bleachers shimmer, Charlotte sat between Priya and a boy named Marcus who had cried at the winter concert and was now crying again, discreetly, into his sleeve. She passed him a tissue from the sleeve of her gown without looking, and he took it without looking, and that small machination of kindness passed between them the way such things do, unannounced. When the principal read her name, her mother's camera flash went off three times, too early, and her father stood up in the fifth row before anyone else in the row did, hands in his pockets, then out of them, then in again.

Afterward, in the parking lot, the deferral still undecided in her pocket like a stone, Charlotte found Priya by the chain-link fence. "Beginning a new status," Charlotte said. "Bachelor or master."

"Or intern," Priya said.

"Or intern." Charlotte turned her cap over in her hands, the tangle of the tassel catching the light. "I still don't know which one, though. That part they don't put in the word."

"They don't," Priya agreed. She took the bobby pins out of Charlotte's hair, one at a time, and dropped them into the cup of her palm. "You've got until Monday to call them. Come on, your mom's holding cake hostage until you get in the picture."

Charlotte followed her across the hot asphalt, cap in hand, and behind them the empty stadium doors swung slowly shut on their own.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A metronome marking of 60 means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second.
story:
The band room smelled like cork grease and old carpet, and Nevaeh had been alone in it for forty minutes, failing at the same sixteen bars. The solo in the Holst suite was supposed to flutter, all sixteenth notes in the upper register of her oboe, and every time she pushed the tempo her tongue tangled and her fingers arrived late, as if they were getting their instructions from somewhere far away.

Marcus came in for his trumpet, saw her red-faced over the reed, and dropped into the chair beside her. "You're rushing the hard part," he said. "Everybody does. My teacher says don't pathologize it, it's just hands being slower than ambition." He pulled her metronome across the stand and dialed it down until the numbers stopped somewhere near the bottom.

"Sixty," he said, tapping the casing. "That means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second."

She had assumed practice meant playing it correctly at performance speed, over and over, until correctness took. That was her mother's philosophy, applied to piano at age eight and chemistry now: repetition at full difficulty builds character. Marcus believed the opposite, that you earned speed the way you earned trust, in small, boring increments, starting from wherever you actually were. She had always thought his way sounded like an excuse for going slow. Now she set her lips to the reed and played the passage with one note per tick, and it was so slow it embarrassed her, every sixteenth note landing on a second like a dropped coin.

But nothing tangled. The fingering that had been impossible was merely easy, and that difference felt like a trick being played on her. She raised the tempo by eights, and at seventy-two her tongue slipped on the turn, so she went back down, and the little weight on top of the metronome swung left and right through the silence like a tiny metronome of its own. Through the high windows the late light came down in a diaphanous column, catching the dust the percussive chaos of fourth period had left in the air.

"You know what my grandma says," Marcus said, feet up on a chair. "Slow is smooth and smooth is fast. Her whole generation is built on some aphorism like that." Nevaeh rolled her eyes at him, but quietly, because the saying had just proved itself on her own reed, and it was annoying when wisdom arrived in a form you could get embroidered on a pillow.

By the time the custodian's cart squeaked past in the hallway, she could play the passage cleanly at ninety-two, still short of the printed one hundred twelve, and she understood something she could not yet say in a sentence. Her mother's way was not wrong; the piece did demand eventual speed, and pretending otherwise would be its own kind of cowardice. But speed was a result, not a method, and treating a method like a result was why she had spent three nights in a row quitting early and calling herself talentless. She could hold both ideas now without either one cancelling the other, though she still wasn't sure what to do on the days when slow practice stopped feeling like patience and started feeling like defeat. That part she would have to find out the same way she had found this out, one second at a time.

She packed the oboe, swabbing the bore, easing the reed into its little plastic coffin. At the door she paused, then went back, set the metronome to sixty, and played the sixteen bars once more, slow and perfect, the tick and the notes locking together like a latch.

"One beat per second," she said to Marcus, and turned out the lights.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by delaying ovulation, and they are more effective the sooner they are taken after unprotected sex.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around Mr. Okafor's arm until the needle on the gauge trembled and settled, and Aiden watched it the way he was learning to watch it, not for a number but for the moment the sound returned. He let the pressure fall slowly through the stethoscope, listening for the first soft knock of the pulse and then the last one. "One twenty-eight over eighty-two," he said, and Mr. Okafor, who ran the waterfront and taught the first-aid elective, raised an eyebrow as if to ask whether that meant anything. Aiden swallowed. "The first number's when your heart contracts. The second's when it rests. High over time, and your arteries take a beating. Salt pushes it up. Regular exercise pulls it down, and so does losing a little weight, but that takes months, not a weekend." It was the longest sentence Aiden had said aloud all summer, and Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard and told him he'd pass the practical if he stopped gripping the bulb like it owed him money.

Aiden had come to Camp Wren as a counselor-in-training mostly because his mother thought it would burnish his college applications, a word she used so often it had begun to sound like furniture. He privately considered the whole CIT wardrobe an affectation, the whistle and the lanyard and the laminated name tag, and he wore them with the reluctant precision of someone playing a part he hadn't auditioned for. Still, the first-aid training was real. Numbers either added up or they didn't, and the body was a machine with readable gauges, and that steadied him in a way that canoe instruction and camp songs did not.

On Thursday evening Priya found him at the picnic tables behind the infirmary, where he was practicing with the cuff on his own arm. She sat down across from him and folded her hands and did not look insouciant the way she usually did, chin up, ready to make a joke of anything. She looked like someone doing arithmetic she didn't want to finish. "Something happened with Josh on the lake trip," she said quietly. "The condom broke. Two nights ago. I've been trying to figure out what to do since then and everyone here would know by breakfast."

"Two nights," Aiden repeated. The number sat in his chest like a stone, because the first-aid manual had taught him that with almost everything, minutes mattered, and he had assumed this would be the same or worse. "Is there a pharmacy in Millbrook?" Millbrook was the town seven miles down the county road, and the camp van went only on Saturdays.

"There's one, I looked it up. But I don't even know if it's too late, or what I'd ask for, or whether they'd call anyone." Priya was seventeen like him, and both of them knew exactly what their parents had said, in different ways, about situations like this. His father's position had always been that knowledge of certain things was itself a kind of permission. Priya's mother, he gathered, had a different but equally firm position. Neither position was standing at a picnic table at nine at night needing an answer.

Aiden had spent the summer learning that a reading meant nothing without knowing what changed it, and the habit of that thinking moved in him now, arranging what he knew from what he didn't. "The van's out," he said. "But there are bikes behind the maintenance shed, and lights on the road the whole way. I'll go with you if you want. If we leave now we're back before eleven." He was already standing, and the cuff slid off his arm and coiled on the bench like something shed.

They rode in the dark with headlamps, Priya's front wheel sometimes brushing his, the frogs in the ditches going quiet and then starting again behind them. At the pharmacy a night clerk with reading glasses unlocked the case, and when Priya asked her question in a voice smaller than any Aiden had heard her use, the clerk answered briefly, glancing at the box. "You want the emergency contraceptive. It works mainly by delaying ovulation, so the sooner you take it after unprotected sex, the more effective it is. Two days is still within the window, but every day counts." Priya bought it, and outside under the buzzing sign she read the leaflet by the light of their headlamps, and Aiden turned away to give her the minute she seemed to need, and drank from his water bottle, and watched a moth throw itself at the light.

On the ride back she was quiet, then said, "So it doesn't end a pregnancy, it just holds the door shut early," and Aiden said that was his understanding of what the clerk meant, and neither of them pretended to be surer than they were. He thought of the gauge and the two numbers, and how the body gave you readings but not guarantees, and how you acted anyway, on the best information, in the time you had. At the camp gate Priya stopped her bike and looked at him. "Thank you for not making it weird." "I probably made it a little weird," Aiden said, and she laughed for real, the first time in three days, and they walked the bikes into the shadows past the sleeping infirmary.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice.
story:
The debate about the third period had started, as most things in Mr. Okafor's classroom started, with Marcus leaning back in his chair and saying something he had not fully thought through. "If a president is doing a good job, why can't he just keep running? Wouldn't the people decide?" Mr. Okafor, who disliked answering questions he thought students could dismantle on their own, wrote parliamentary on one side of the board and presidential on the other, and said nothing. Jordan, three rows back, recognized the silence as an assignment.

Jordan wanted the scholarship to the summer program in political science, and the application asked for an essay comparing how a parliamentary system and a presidential system each choose and remove a head of government. He had written two pages already, both of them, he suspected, wrong in ways he could not yet name. Now Marcus had handed him the exact question his essay kept circling. He pulled his legal pad out from under his chemistry folder and began a list: PM chosen by the party, president chosen by the voters. PM removed by a vote of no confidence, president removed by impeachment. He stared at the list, waiting for it to become an argument, and it refused.

"Jordan," Mr. Okafor said, without turning from the board. "You've been writing for four minutes. Say something."

He had not expected to be called on, and the page in front of him was still just two columns. "In a parliamentary system," he said slowly, "the head of government isn't elected by the whole country. The party picks the prime minister, and the parliament can remove him whenever he loses their support. A vote of no confidence. So it's faster. But it means the voters never chose him directly."

"And presidents?" Marcus asked, still tipped back in his chair.

"Directly elected. Fixed terms. But here's what I keep getting stuck on." Jordan tapped his pen against the pad. "Removal is supposed to be hard. Impeachment takes a whole machinery, a whole process. It's not designed to be quick."

"Which is better?" Priya asked from the window row, and Jordan said, honestly, "I don't know yet," and a few people laughed, but Mr. Okafor didn't.

At lunch, Jordan found Marcus by the vending machines, holding a bag of chips he wasn't eating. "Your question this morning," Jordan said. "The popular president running forever. I looked it up during study hall. The 22nd Amendment to the Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice."

Marcus frowned at his chips. "So even if everybody wanted him?"

"Even then. Twice, and that's it." Jordan watched Marcus turn this over, watched him arrive somewhere. "So it's a third thing," Marcus said. "Not choosing, not removing. A limit that happens before either one. Like the system doesn't totally trust popularity."

Jordan wrote that down on his hand because his legal pad was in his locker. That afternoon, sitting on the bleachers behind the gym with the essay open on his laptop, he remembered his grandfather, who had told a story every Thanksgiving about a council in the village where he grew up, how the elders could stand up at any meeting and withdraw their confidence in the man who spoke for them, and how the speaker would simply walk home before dinner. Jordan had been eleven and had thought it sounded brutal. His grandfather had said, "It wasn't brutal. It was ordinary. He'd be back the next week, arguing again, just not standing in front." He had liked watching his grandfather introspect in that slow way of his, turning a memory over before releasing it. It occurred to Jordan now, with the laptop warm on his knees, that he had been raised on two vocabularies without noticing: the fixed and the flexible, the term and the confidence.

He tried to put both on the page. The presidential system, he wrote, makes the head of government rigid in office, protected by fixed terms and a difficult removal, and the parliamentary system leaves the same figure ductile, shaped continuously by the parliament that made him. Then he deleted "shaped continuously" because it sounded like a thesaurus. He kept "ductile" because it was the true word, and because the essay was supposed to sound like him.

His younger sister, Devi, found him there after her soccer practice, backpack still on, and read over his shoulder with the shamelessness of a ninth grader. "So the prime minister can just be fired? By his own people?"

"Not fired exactly. Removed. If parliament votes no confidence, he has to go."

"That seems worse for him."

"It might be better for everyone else," Jordan said. "That's the part I haven't figured out. Whether stability is the same thing as safety." He looked at the screen, at the sentence he had just typed, and left it there, unresolved, with a colon after it and nothing following, a small hole he had decided not to fill with something easy.

Mr. Okafor, passing the bleachers on his way to the parking lot, paused with his keys in his hand. "The essay for the scholarship?" he asked, and Jordan nodded. "If a pedagogue tells you the answer, it isn't yours," Okafor said. "I'm told I have a reputation. Try to keep my fingerprints off it." He walked on toward his gray sedan.

Devi sat down beside him, unzipping the backpack, producing two granola bars and handing him one. Jordan took it, typed a question mark into the hole in his paragraph, and then deleted the question mark too, leaving the sentence bare. Somewhere across the field the sprinklers came on, ticking across the grass in slow arcs, and he hit save.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Sorting a list takes more work than one linear search, so sorting just to run binary search pays off only when the same data will be searched many times.
story:
The basement smelled like damp carpet and microwave popcorn, and Theo's laptop had been wheezing since October, so moribund was really the only word for it. Jaxon sat cross-legged on the floor with his own machine balanced on a chemistry textbook, a blank file open in the editor. In nine days they had to submit their project for the regional coding competition, a program that looked up students in a roster of two thousand names, and Jaxon had never written anything this large. He had, until tonight, never written a class at all.

"You're hiding the data," Theo said, leaning over from the beanbag. "Watch. Private fields. Then the only way in is through the getter."

"That seems paranoid," Jaxon said.

"It's polite. The class keeps its own house, and you knock."

So Jaxon typed, slowly, checking every brace. He made a Student class with private fields for name and ID, then a getName method that handed the name back, then a setter for the ID because Mr. Okafor's spec said IDs could change after enrollment. He wrote a test, three lines in a main method, and ran it, and for once nothing turned red. The little green run bar appeared and he sat very still, feeling something in his chest unknot.

Priya arrived at nine with her board games she had no intention of playing and a bag of sour candy. She pulled up the roster spec on her phone and frowned. "It says here we search for one name. One lookup, then the program prints the record and quits."

"Then we sort it," Theo said immediately. "Sorted list, binary search, that's the smart way. You cut the list in half over and over."

"Sorting two thousand names is a lot of work for one lookup," Priya said. "I think we just walk the list start to finish. One linear search."

"A linear search sounds like giving up," Theo said. "Anybody can walk a list."

They argued around the ping-pong table for ten minutes, the kind of argument where both people are mostly defending their pride. Jaxon said nothing. He kept thinking about the green bar, about how the class kept its own house, and about what his grandmother always said, a maxim she repeated so often he could hear her voice: do the work once if the work only happens once.

At 9:40 Priya's phone buzzed, and she read the text out loud because it was from their fourth teammate, DeShawn, who was home with the flu.

"Tell them my decision," she read. "Sorting takes more work than one linear search. Way more. So sorting just so we can run a binary search only pays off if we're going to search the same data many times. We search once. One and done. I vote we walk the list. Also I am dying, send soup."

"That's not a real vote if you can't be here," Theo said, but without heat.

"It's a real vote," Jaxon said. "It's also right." He turned his laptop so they could both see. "Look at my test. I wrote the class so the fields are private, so nobody touches the data directly. The class decides how things get done and the outside world just asks. That's what we should do with the search. The smart way isn't the fancy way. It's the way that matches how many times you'll actually use it."

Theo slumped back into the beanbag and blew out a long breath. "Fine. But if the judges see linear search and think we're amateurs?"

"Then we comment the code," Priya said. "We write, this list is searched once, so one linear search costs less than sorting it. DeShawn can draft that from his deathbed."

Jaxon smiled at that, but he kept typing. Because there was one thing he had not said out loud, and it sat in his stomach like a swallowed stone: he had checked the fine print on the spec, a later page, and there was a line about an optional feature, a "future extension" allowing repeated lookups if a user typed more than one name. If they implemented that, the searching would happen many times, and then the whole calculus flipped, and sorting would be worth it after all. He could not tell yet whether the judges would ever run that extension, or whether it was a trap for teams that overbuilt.

"Hey," he said. "Before we lock this in."

Both of them looked at him. The laptop fan hummed, the furnace ticked somewhere above, and on screen his little Student class waited, private and patient, guarding its two fields.

"There's a line on page six," Jaxon said, and turned the screen toward them.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
Naomi set her phone face-down beside her plate before her mother could say anything about it, which meant she spent the first ten minutes of dinner not hearing a word. Her uncle Ravi was holding forth about his neighbor's fence, garrulous as always, and her little cousin was dropping peas one by one onto the floor with the patience of a scientist, but Naomi kept seeing Dev's slide deck. Slide fourteen. The math was wrong in a way she'd caught at eleven the night before, and she had said nothing, and neither had anyone else on the team of five, and the presentation was Thursday.

"Earth to Naomi," her mother said. "You've cut your chicken into a grid."

"Sorry. Group project."

"Ah," her uncle said, delighted, as if she'd offered him a topic. "Group projects. The great character-building scam. I did all the work in every group I was ever in, and I turned out fine."

"You turned out garrulous," her mother said, and everyone laughed, including the pea scientist.

Naomi laughed too, and then stopped, because something about the joke snagged on the actual problem. It wasn't that she'd have to do all the work. It was that all five of them had looked at slide fourteen, she was nearly sure, and all five had decided that pointing it out was more dangerous than letting it sit there. She knew Marcus had rewritten his section twice without saying why. She knew Priya had asked, in the chat, whether everyone was "feeling good about the numbers," which was not a question, and no one had answered it, including her.

She turned her phone over and searched the phrase that had been circling her all day, the one her econ teacher had mentioned offhand last spring and then never returned to: teams afraid to admit mistakes. The first result was a study. She read a line of it twice, then a third time.

"Naomi."

"One second. This is actually important."

"No phones at the table is an injunction, not a suggestion," her mother said, but she said it mildly, and she leaned sideways to look, because her mother could never not look.

"There was a researcher," Naomi said, mostly to the table now, because she'd realized halfway through the second read that she wanted witnesses. "Amy Edmondson. In 1999 she described this thing where a team shares a belief that it's safe to take interpersonal risks. Like admitting a mistake. She gave it a name."

"What name?" her cousin asked, from underneath the table, where the peas lived.

"It's called psychological safety," Naomi said.

"Sounds like a wellness app," her uncle said.

"No, it's the opposite of a wellness app, it's whether people on a team can say 'I messed up' without the floor opening." She was talking fast now, which she did when two ideas were snapping together. "That's us. That's our group. Marcus redid his whole section in silence. Priya asked if we were 'feeling good' about the numbers. Nobody said the numbers were wrong, because we're all protecting ourselves from looking like the dumb one, and meanwhile the dumb thing is still in the deck."

Her mother refilled her water glass without being asked, a small kindness Naomi registered even mid-sentence.

"So what do you do," her uncle said. "March in and announce the team lacks psychological safety?"

"That's the part I keep getting wrong in my head." She pulled her fork through the rice, making a channel. "If I open with the theory, it's a lecture, and it makes it worse, like I'm diagnosing them. My dad always says feedback should be specific and kind, and I used to think that was a dodge, like the 'compliment sandwich.' But I think the specific part is the honest part and the kind part is the delivery, and they're not opposites. I could say, 'I found an error on slide fourteen, I almost missed it myself, can we fix it together.' That's true and it gives Dev a way to hear it."

"And if Dev's defensive anyway?"

"Then I don't know," Naomi said, and found she meant it without despair. "That's the part no study fixes. Maybe it's a risk you just take, which is sort of the point of the whole thing."

She ate three bites in a row, actually tasting them for the first time, then picked the phone back up and typed a message to Dev: found something on slide 14, not a big fix, want to look together tomorrow at lunch? She put the phone face-down again and watched it, face-down, as if she could see through it.

Under the table, her cousin released one final pea.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In England and Wales, a landlord must place a tenant's deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of receiving it.
story:
Jordyn had spread the letting agent's paperwork across the kitchen table like a crime scene, which was roughly how she thought of it. Three flats, three fees, and a mother on the other side of the kettle saying things like "in my day you just paid the first month and moved in." The kettle ticked as it cooled. On the laptop screen, waiting patiently in a separate window, was Marcus, who had been renting in Manchester since September and who had called to ask her opinion of something he called "a bit weird, probably nothing."

She put him on speaker and picked up the first form. "Rent's twelve hundred a month here," she said. "Which is fine. Which is technically fine, if I take the campus job and never buy anything again." Marcus laughed, because his rent in Manchester was less, and because he liked reminding her. She read on. "They also want a deposit. Five weeks of rent, held against damage. That's nearly fifteen hundred up front before I've slept a single night there."

"That's the thing, actually," Marcus said. "My deposit. I paid it in August and I never got any paperwork about it. No certificate, no letter, nothing. I keep meaning to ask if that's normal and then I keep not asking."

Jordyn dug a pen out of the drawer, the one that still worked, and wrote deposit, Marcus, no paperwork on the back of an electricity bill. It joined a growing list of things she was supposed to be looking into instead of looking at flats. Her mother set down a mug of tea at her elbow and drifted back to the hob, in the way of mothers who want to be available but not involved.

"Have you looked it up?" Jordyn asked. She was already typing, one-handed, deposit England tenant no paperwork. The results assembled themselves with the cheerful efficiency of the internet telling you something you should have known months ago. She read for a moment, then sat back. "Okay. So this is actually a thing. In England and Wales a landlord has to put your deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of receiving it."

There was a pause on the line, the small crackly kind. "Thirty days," Marcus said slowly, as if testing the weight of it. "And he didn't do that? Or he did and just never told me?"

"Either way, there's paperwork that should exist and doesn't." Jordyn heard herself say it and noticed, distantly, that she was enjoying this, the small clean pleasure of a rule that somebody somewhere had written down and that Marcus's landlord had apparently not read. "You should ask him for it. In writing. Nicely, at first." She could picture Marcus nodding in his room above the chip shop, surrounded by unpacked boxes he had promised his mother he would exhume over Christmas, a promise she had heard him break in real time over the phone.

Her mother spoke from the hob without turning around. "When your father and I bought this house, the deposit was the whole battle. Down payment, they call it. Ten percent of the price, up front, before the bank will lend you the rest." She stirred something that did not need stirring. "A mortgage is just renting money from a bank for twenty-five years, except at the end you own the bricks."

"That's cheerful," Jordyn said. But she wrote it down too, because the comparison had a shape she wanted to keep: the deposit she might never see again versus the down payment that turned into a house. Both of them were doors that only opened if you could produce a pile of money first, and the pile was the whole difference between the people who got through and the people who stood outside holding forms. She looked at the three flats on the table, then at Marcus's pixelated face, and understood that these were the same problem wearing different coats, and that the law about protection schemes was one of the few places where somebody had noticed and drawn a line.

"I'll email him tonight," Marcus said. "The landlord. I'll say I'm just checking where the deposit's being held." He sounded braver than he had ten minutes ago, though not by much, and Jordyn decided not to point this out. There was a limit to how loquacious you could be with someone who was working up to a difficult email.

"Ask for the certificate," she said. "And forward me whatever he sends. Or whatever he doesn't." She was already drafting the message in her head for him, knowing he would never send her version, knowing he would send a shorter, apologetic one that said sorry to bother you somewhere in the first line. That was Marcus. The epidemiology of his problems was consistent: they spread quietly and were caught late, usually by someone else.

Her mother set her own mug down across the table and sat, which meant the flat-hunting portion of the evening had officially merged into the life-lecture portion, and Jordyn closed the laptop lid to half, muting Marcus mid-sentence about chip shop opening hours. The kitchen went quiet except for the fridge.

"So which flat is it going to be?" her mother asked.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: The citric acid cycle turns twice for each glucose molecule, because one glucose produces two acetyl-CoA molecules and each enters the cycle separately.
story:
Chloe spread her notes across the kitchen table the way her mother laid out legal briefs, each page squared to the table's edge, and she had been at it for forty minutes before her brother came in and put his elbows directly on the translation diagram. She was trying to learn, before Monday's entrance exam, how DNA becomes protein, and she could recite it now, transcription then translation, the copying of the gene into RNA, the reading of that RNA into amino acids, but reciting and understanding were turning out to be different animals. Marcus, who was eleven and mercurial, forever swinging between sulking and showing off, dropped a plastic dinosaur onto her paper and said, "Teach me."

"You'll be bored in a minute."

"Teach me anyway. I'll pay you a dollar."

She could use a dollar, and more than that she had read somewhere that the surest way to find the holes in your own understanding was to explain something to someone who kept asking why. So she pulled the diagram out from under his elbows and smoothed it. "Okay. It's like a recipe book," she said. "The DNA stays in the kitchen, in the nucleus. You don't want to get the book dirty, so you copy out one page. That's the RNA. The copy goes out to where the cooking happens, and the cooks read it three letters at a time and build a protein." Marcus picked up the dinosaur and made it walk across the double helix. "Who's the cook?"

"The ribosome. Now pay attention, because this is the part I keep getting wrong." She flipped to her second sheet, the one with the arrow diagram of glucose being broken down, and there the trouble was waiting for her again, the same wrong number she had gotten in practice tests twice tonight. "After the copying," she said, more to herself now, "the cell burns the sugar for energy, and you count up the energy made, the ATP, and my count keeps coming out short. Every time."

Marcus, from Chloe's point of view, was a pest who had learned, or perhaps habituated himself, to interrupt her the moment she got close to anything fragile in her own head. What she did not see, from across the table, was that he was actually reading the diagram. He followed the arrows with his finger, the way he followed dungeon maps in his games, and he noticed something she had been staring straight through. "Why does it split here?" he asked. "One line comes in and then there's two of this triangle thing after it."

She looked where he was pointing. One glucose, and after the first stage there were two of the little two-carbon units, and every arrow after that point belonged to each of them, not just one. The citric acid cycle turned twice for every glucose that entered, because each glucose yielded two acetyl-CoA molecules and each one went into the cycle separately. Everything after glycolysis happened twice, and she had been counting it once. "That's it," she said. "That's why my count is wrong. It's all happening two times."

"So you owe me a dollar."

"That's not how tutoring works."

"It's exactly how it works. I found the split."

Their mother came through with a stack of folders and set a subpoena on the counter, some document that had to go out in the morning mail, and Chloe caught her eye and said, "Mom, tell him finding a bug in my notes isn't the same as understanding them." Their mother, who had learned not to referee before coffee, said, "Tell me what a protein is first, and then I'll rule on the dollar."

From where Marcus sat, watching his sister gather the pages back toward herself, it seemed to him that she had gone somewhere else for a moment, the way she did, and that he had put her there. "A protein is what the whole thing is for," she said slowly. "The DNA is the archive. The RNA is the message. The protein is the thing that actually does the work in the cell. And the sugar is the fuel that pays for all of it, and you have to count the fuel right or you think the cell is poorer than it is." She looked at the diagram again, at the single line splitting into two, and she could not quite say which was truer, that the cell was one story or that it was two stories told at once, and she decided she was allowed not to know that yet.

"The dollar," Marcus said.

She dug in the pocket of her hoodie and found a crumpled bill and put it on the table between them, holding two fingers on one corner of it. "You get this when you can tell me why the count was wrong."

He looked at the diagram, at the two triangles, and she watched him actually think, his mouth a little open, the dinosaur forgotten on its side. "Because after it splits," he said, "the circle part, the citric acid cycle, it has to go around for both of them. Two times for one sugar." She let go of the dollar, and he snatched it and was out of the kitchen, and she sat back down and picked up her pen and drew, in the margin, a small circle with an arrow going around it twice.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The '10 percent rule', never raising weekly running distance more than 10 percent, is a popular guideline, but studies have not shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans.
story:
Leo arrived at the field at seven with a whiteboard under one arm and his chemistry notes folded into his back pocket, the enthalpy diagrams half finished, because the exam was Monday and the tournament was Saturday and both refused to move. He set the whiteboard against the goalpost. Twelve eleven-year-olds, and their problem was simple to see and hard to fix: they passed to wherever a teammate had been standing two seconds ago, not where he was running. Three weeks Leo had been watching them, and now Coach Ruiz had a wedding to attend, and the team was Leo's until Saturday.

"We're doing passing drills," he told them when they gathered. "Not scrimmaging. Passing."

Groans. A kid named Marcus, the smallest one, didn't groan, just looked at the ground.

"Watch." Leo drew three cones on the whiteboard, spaced in a triangle, then an arrow between the second and third. "The ball goes where he's going to be. Not where he is."

Dani arrived halfway through the first drill, jogging the perimeter of the field the way he did every morning, tracking his weekly mileage like other people tracked money. During water break he dropped onto the bench beside Leo, phone out, scrolling his training app.

"How's the science project going," Leo said.

"You mean the team? It's fine."

"Your mileage. Your plan."

Dani turned the phone toward him. A graph, rising in neat steps. "The 10 percent rule," he said, like it was a law of physics. "Never raise weekly running distance more than 10 percent. That's how you build a season without breaking yourself."

Leo looked at the graph. Neat, ordered, undeniable, the way enthalpy diagrams were undeniable, and he thought of his own plan for the kids, adding one new layer to the drills each practice, small increments, because increments felt like safety. That was the whole logic of his whiteboard. He took out his phone and typed, partly to allay the worry that he was building Saturday's plan on a guess.

The search results were not what he expected. He read one, then another, then a third, holding the screen at an angle so Dani could see it.

"What," Dani said.

"It says it's a popular guideline," Leo said slowly. "But the studies haven't shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans."

Dani took the phone. Read it again himself, thumb hovering, not scrolling. "That can't be right. Everyone says it."

"Everyone says pass to the feet, too. Look where that's gotten them." Leo tipped his chin toward the field, where a ball had just rolled out of bounds because the receiver had stopped moving and the passer had led him anyway. "Maybe gradual is gradual. Maybe the 10 percent thing isn't magic, it's just, you know. One version of careful."

Dani gave the phone back and didn't answer, which for Dani was an answer. He stood, stretched, and started his second lap.

Marcus had watched the whole exchange from the end of the water line, close enough to hear the phone part, though he didn't understand most of it. What he understood was this: Leo had looked something up, and the looking-up had changed his face, and now Leo was staring at the whiteboard like it had lied to him. Marcus didn't like the drills. They made him feel slow, because he was slow, and because the cones made it obvious. But he'd also noticed, during the triangle drill, that when he ran to the empty cone before the ball came, it arrived right at his feet, and for one second he'd looked like the best player on the field.

"Leo," he called, because it seemed like the moment.

Leo looked over.

"When we do it slow, it works. When we do it fast, it stops working."

"Then we go slower first," Leo said. He walked to the whiteboard, erased the arrow he'd drawn for Thursday, and drew a shorter one. He'd been treating his progression like Dani treated mileage, some fixed increment that would guarantee improvement by Saturday, and now he understood that the increment itself wasn't the guarantee, only the caution behind it was. What he still didn't know, and said so to nobody, was how much caution eleven-year-olds actually needed, and whether Saturday would punish him for going too slow as surely as for going too fast.
