"Line up," he called. "Triangle. Half speed. I want the passer calling the name before the ball moves."

They ran it half speed and it was ugly, balls wobbling, two kids colliding at the far cone. Leo made them run it again. And again. On the fourth attempt, a boy named Tomas played the ball into open space ahead of Marcus, and Marcus was already there, already running, and trapped it clean with the inside of his foot.

"There," Leo said. "That. Do that again."

Dani finished his lap and stopped at the sideline, breathing hard, phone still in his hand, screen dark.

"We're going full speed on Saturday," Leo told him, not looking away from the triangle.

"Even with the slow week?"

Leo watched the ball move, watched Marcus start his run before anyone passed to him. "Full speed. We'll find out together."

Dani sat down on the bench and opened his training app.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
story:
The community hall smelled of sesame oil and steam from the rice cookers lined up along the back wall, and Layla stood near the folding tables with a paper plate of dumplings she wasn't eating. Her mother had already drifted toward the mahjong corner, leaving Layla with her nine-year-old cousin Mei, who was counting something in her pocket with the concentration of an ascetic who had just discovered temptation.

"Nine dollars," Mei announced. "Auntie Po gave me three dollars in this one and Grandma gave me six, but Grandma's envelope is redder, see?"

Layla looked. Both envelopes were red, but Grandma's was the deep, lacquered red of the shrine cabinets at the front of the hall, the red that Mei said, matter-of-factly, meant good luck and kept evil away. Layla had known that much since she was small, though she hadn't known, until tonight, that the envelopes were for children and unmarried younger relatives, which she'd overheard Auntie Po explaining to Mr. Delgado from the insurance office, who had come for the food and stayed for the generosity. Layla turned the phrase over while Mei bounded off toward the lion dance practice. Unmarried younger relatives. She was sixteen. She was, technically, all three of those things, and yet she felt like a person collecting a toll for a bridge she'd already crossed.

Her phone buzzed. A message from Daniel, who was across the hall by the door, visibly weighing whether to come in.

"Is it weird if I'm here? I don't know anyone except you."

"Not weird. Bring a plate. Say happy new year to anyone over fifty and they'll adopt you."

"Should I bow? What do I do with my hands?"

"Daniel. It's a community hall, not a ceremony. Come eat a dumpling."

She watched him read this, watched him square his shoulders the way he did before a piano recital, and felt, briefly, fond of him in a way she didn't plan to say out loud.

The trouble arrived with Auntie Po, who moved down the table dispensing envelopes like a dealer at a generous card game. When she reached Layla she paused, envelope hovering, and said, "Still in school? No ring on that finger?" Then she pressed the red paper into Layla's hand before Layla could answer, and moved on to a boy of eleven, and Layla stood there holding it. She had spent the past hour composing, in her head, a graceful refusal, something about being too old, about saving it for Mei, about how a person who paid her own bus fare probably shouldn't be collecting lucky money. The speech had been elegant, almost tangential in its indirection, and now it was useless, because the envelope was already in her hand, warm from Auntie Po's pocket, and refusing it now would require her to expostulate in the middle of the hall, which was the one thing worse than accepting.

Daniel appeared beside her with a plate piled absurdly high. "Okay, this is the best thing that has ever happened to me," he said, through a dumpling.

"There's more at the back table."

"There could not be more. There is a finite amount of more."

Layla slid the envelope into her pocket unresolved. She kept circling the question the way Mei circled the lion dancers, approaching and retreating: on one side was the plain fact that she qualified, that the custom said what it said, that Auntie Po had judged her eligible without hesitation; on the other was her own sense that acceptance was a kind of claiming, a childishness she was supposed to be outgrowing. She could not make the two fit together, and she was honest enough with herself to admit it. Maybe, she thought, she could hold both at once: take the envelope as what it was, a gift from an aunt who loved her, and leave the question of what taking it meant for another year, when the answer might be different.

Then Mei came back, breathless, holding out a small envelope of her own, folded badly from red construction paper, sealed with a sticker of a cartoon rabbit. "For you," Mei said. "Because you gave me your dumplings last time when I dropped mine, and it's new year, and I have three dollars."

Layla opened it. Inside was three dollars and a note in Mei's careful handwriting: "You are not too old. Grandma checked."

Daniel leaned over to read it. "Checked with who?"

"Grandma," Layla said, and folded the note closed. She put it in the envelope with the three dollars, and the envelope in her pocket next to Auntie Po's, and only then noticed Auntie Po watching from the far table with an expression of unmistakable satisfaction, as though the whole evening, the envelopes, the red, the luck itself, had been arranged for exactly this moment.

"There," Auntie Po called across the hall. "Now the rabbit gives back."

Layla looked down at the badly folded paper in her hand. "The rabbit," she said, "is keeping this one."

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
The laptop refused to cooperate, and the clock on Grandpa's mantel struck seven with the solid certainty of a clock that had never once cared about anyone's deadlines. Victoria had until midnight to submit the database assignment, and she was spending her evening in a riparian cottage two buses from campus, watching her grandfather's phone screen instead of her own.

"Look at this," Grandpa said, lowering himself into the chair beside her. "From the neighbours. They say the mill race burst this morning and the lower fields are underwater. Karim wants me to post it to the village group before bed, so people move their animals." The video showed brown water sliding over a fence, a shed door flapping, a street she almost recognized. "I don't like it. Something about it doesn't sit right. But I can't say what, and I can't very well accuse a neighbour of machinations without proof."

Victoria had seen something at her mother's office last spring that she hadn't thought about since. A colleague had been checking a clip on his screen and she'd asked what he was doing. "InVID-WeVerify," he'd said, not looking up. She remembered because the name sounded like a plumbing fixture. She had watched him work for a minute before her mother called her away, and what she remembered was a row of images, like film stills, each with search buttons beneath it.

"I might be able to check it," she said. "Wait." She installed the plugin on Grandpa's old browser, chewing the inside of her cheek while it loaded, and when the tab opened she read the small print aloud so they could both hear it. "InVID-WeVerify, a project funded by the European Union." The extension let her drop the video in, and then it did what she remembered: it split the video into key frames, a strip of stills, each one ready to be reverse-searched.

"Those are like fingerprints," she murmured, dragging the first frame, the fence and the flapping door, into the search bar. While it worked, her assignment sat open behind the tab, half a query abandoned on the screen. She'd been at it since four, trying to join a customer table to an orders table and surface the customers who never ordered anything, and every version she wrote either returned everyone or no one. The trick, she was almost sure, was in the join itself, in asking the question from the empty side of it.

The search results came back, and there was the fence. There was the flapping door. The matching page was three years old, from a flood in a river town two valleys over, and the street she'd almost recognized was one she'd seen in a photograph on Grandpa's hallway wall, from a trip before she was born. "It's not our river," she said. "It's an old video wearing our river's clothes."

Grandpa put the phone face down on the table, exhaling through his nose. "So I post nothing. Karim will grumble, but half the village would have been awake all night for nothing." He watched her switch back to the assignment window. "Go on, then. Don't let an old man's flood eat your future."

She went at it differently now. Instead of starting from the customers and asking who had orders, she started from the join itself and let it keep every customer whether or not anything matched, then kept only the rows where the order side came back empty. When she ran it, the result table filled with names, customers with no orders at all, each one surfaced precisely because the other table had nothing to say about them. 11:54 glowed in the corner of the screen. She checked the output twice, attached the file, and pressed submit at 11:58, then sat back with her hands still hovering over the keys, not quite believing the names would still be there when she looked again.

"You look like a woman who won something," Grandpa said.

"Maybe," she said. "Ask me tomorrow." She was already less certain than she sounded; the query was right for tonight's tables, and she had a feeling that the empty side of a join could hide things too, that absence was easier to find than to interpret. She was reaching to close the laptop when his phone buzzed on the table. He squinted at the message and turned it toward her, half laughing. It was the seed catalogue, confirming the twelve packets of sweet peas he had sworn, for weeks, he would never order.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parallel parking, a driver usually reverses in from alongside the car in front, turning the wheel toward the curb first and then away as the car swings into the space.
story:
The laundromat on Delancey had a parking lot with exactly four spaces, two of them always taken by the shop van, and Sara had claimed the remaining corner as her personal driving school. Her mother sat inside behind the window with a paperback, one eye on the dryer and one on the lot, while Sara practiced parallel parking between a traffic cone and a folding chair she had wedged where the curb would be. She was failing at it with a regularity that had begun to feel almost scientific.

"You're crooked again," her mother called through the propped door, not unkindly. "Like a car parking itself sideways out of spite."

Sara got out and looked. The nose of the Honda pointed toward the folding chair at an angle that would have earned her an automatic fail, the kind of angle that made other drivers pity you. She had been turning the wheel the wrong way, she realized, or at the wrong moment, though she could not yet say which. That was the infuriating part: the error was somewhere in the sequence, invisible until it bloomed into crookedness.

She had her reasons for wanting the license by August, and they were not the ones her friends assumed. Not concerts, not freedom in the abstract. Her grandmother's dialysis was Tuesdays and Fridays, and her uncle, who normally drove her, had taken a job in Hartford. Nobody had said the words "you should learn," because nobody in her family said things like that directly; they reified obligation into silences and calendar gaps and the sudden appearance, on the kitchen table, of a practice test booklet. Her mother's maxim, delivered once while folding towels, had been: "We don't ask people to be grateful in this house, we just show up." Sara had found, over the years, that this sounded simpler than it was.

A boy from her school, Marcus, came into the laundromat that afternoon with a garbage bag of laundry and no detergent, having forgotten his, a fact he announced to the room with the cheerfulness of the truly disaffected. He watched Sara from the window while his socks tumbled.

"You're doing it backwards," he said through the screen.

"Thank you, Marcus. Extremely helpful."

"No, I mean the wheel. My sister taught me last summer. You pull up next to the car in front, right, alongside it, and then you back in. You turn the wheel toward the curb first." He mimed it, hands rotating an invisible wheel left. "Then when the car swings into the space, you turn back the other way to straighten out. That's the part you're skipping. You're turning away the whole time, so you just end up diagonal."

Sara sat with that for a second. Toward the curb first, then away. It felt counterintuitive, like being told to lean into a fall, but she had spent forty minutes doing the intuitive thing and it had produced nothing but geometry of shame.

She got back in, pulled forward until she was alongside the folding chair, checked her mirrors, and reversed, turning the wheel toward the curb. When the car had swung partway into the space, she turned the wheel away, and the Honda, obedient for the first time all afternoon, straightened itself against the curb like a sentence ending in a period. She sat there with the engine idling, surprised by how small the correction had been.

"See," Marcus said, mildly.

The highway was the other half of the test, and the harder half for her, though not for the reasons on the checklist. Merging required her to commit: to accelerate down a ramp toward a gap in moving traffic and trust that the gap would hold. Parking, at least, was a negotiation with stationary objects. She thought of her uncle, who had once admitted over Christmas dinner that he had taken the Hartford job partly because he was tired, and she had not known whether to be angry at him for the honesty or grateful for it, and had settled, as usual, on neither. Perhaps commitment was like the wheel: you could not tell, until you were inside the maneuver, whether you had turned too early or too late.

She practiced the merge that evening on Route 9 with her mother in the passenger seat, hands rigid on the armrest. The ramp, the acceleration, the glance over her shoulder, the slide into the lane between a pickup and a bakery van. Her mother exhaled.

"That was fine," her mother said. "That was actually fine."

"Say it like you mean it."

"I mean it like I mean it. Tuesday, you drive your grandmother."

Tuesday was four days away, and the test itself was not until September, which meant one of them would have to sit in the dialysis parking lot for three hours, and Sara understood that this was the family's way of asking her to choose. She signaled, checked her mirror, and eased into the right lane.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: False friends are words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning; Spanish 'embarazada' means pregnant, not embarrassed.
story:
The festival had taken over the whole park by noon, but Amelia had not come for the food trucks or the dancers. She had come for the blue tent at the far end, where the Spanish debate table was folded, with a sign-up sheet and a kitchen timer, five minutes per speaker, entirely in Spanish. Her mother had signed the permission slip without reading it carefully, assuming it was the folk-dance workshop. Amelia had not corrected her.

Her topic was whether phones should be allowed in schools, which she had argued twice already in English, once for and once against. Her coach believed in picking a side and holding it until the timer ran out. Her grandmother, who had raised three children without a single device in the house, believed phones were rotting attention spans outright, that the mind would atrophy if you fed it nothing but screens. Amelia had spent two weeks trying to get underneath both positions, writing phrases on index cards at the kitchen table while her grandmother stirred soup and muttered.

She was third on the list. The first speaker, a college boy with a lanyard, spoke fluidly about digital literacy, and the second, a girl from Amelia's own school named Rosa, argued the grandmother's side with real fire. Then came the fourth slot, a boy everyone called Teo, who was visibly nervous and spoke faster as the timer went on. He was describing a school policy, and Amelia caught most of it, until he said, leaning forward, "Los estudiantes se sienten muy embarazados," and the small audience broke into laughter, a ripple of it, and a woman near the front hid her mouth with her hand.

Teo stopped dead. His face went red and he sat down without using his last minute, folding his arms like a child told to wait outside. Amelia leaned toward Rosa, who was still smirking. "What did he say?"

"Embarazado. He meant embarrassed. But embarazada means pregnant. He told everyone the students feel very pregnant."

"That's cruel, kind of," Amelia said, but she wrote it down on the back of an index card, because her own notes had the word in them too, circled twice, and her stomach turned at how close she had come.

The moderator called her name. The woman who had laughed caught Amelia's sleeve as she stood. "False friends," the woman said, tapping Amelia's card without reading it, as if she'd guessed. "Words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning. They get everyone eventually." She let go and turned back to the table.

Amelia stood at the podium and the timer clicked, and she began in Spanish, slower than she had practiced, each sentence placed rather than thrown. She argued that phones in schools were neither poison nor freedom, that her grandmother was right that attention could be lost and her coach was right that banning things taught nothing, that the real question was who taught students to use the tool, and that she did not yet know how schools could do this at scale. She said the last part plainly, "no sé todavía," and noticed that saying it in Spanish made the uncertainty feel less like defeat than like a door left open. She used her final thirty seconds to concede a counterargument she could not answer, because it seemed more honest than pretending.

When the timer buzzed, there was scattered applause and no laughter. Teo was watching her from across the tent, arms still folded, though less tightly now. Rosa came over afterward. "You said you didn't know. In a debate."

"I didn't," Amelia said. "I still don't."

They gave out ribbons at four o'clock, blue ones, and Amelia did not win one; a graduate student with the manner of an aesthete, praising the music of Teo's broken sentence before Teo's own turn, took first place. Amelia found Teo at the empanada stand instead, holding a plate he hadn't touched. She showed him her index card, embarazado crossed out, embarazada written above it, and said, in her careful, slow Spanish, "I almost said it too."

He looked at the card, then at her, and something in his shoulders let go. "Next year," he said, "I'm saying it on purpose. First sentence."

"First sentence," Amelia agreed, and tore the card in half and dropped it in the bin between them.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: After a LEFT JOIN, COUNT of an orders column gives 0 for customers without orders, but COUNT(*) gives 1, because it counts the NULL-filled row.
story:
The repair shop smelled of solder and lemon wipes, and Mackenzie was behind the counter because Deshawn had called in sick, which meant she handled customers alone until noon. She was eighteen and saving for a laptop before September, and so far the morning had produced one cracked screen, one waterlogged tablet, and a boy named Percy from her old statistics class who came in every Tuesday with his Chromebook and sat by the register doing homework while his mother worked two doors down at the dental office.

Today Percy had his database assignment open, and his report said something wrong. The shop's owner, Mr. Okonkwo, kept a whiteboard behind the counter for tracking repairs, and Percy kept glancing at it like it might help. "It says every customer ordered at least once," he said. "The teacher gave us a sample database. Thirty customers. I got thirty."

Mackenzie looked up from the tray of screws she was sorting. "Every one?"

"Every one." He turned the Chromebook toward her. She saw two tables, Customers and Orders, and a query with LEFT JOIN in it, which she recognized because she'd spent the whole previous week teaching herself SQL from a library book, in preparation for a class she was taking in the fall. "You're counting wrong," she said.

"I'm counting with COUNT," Percy said. "That's the whole point of the function."

She wiped her hands on her jeans and came around the counter. The screen had his query in a plain text editor, and beneath it the result grid with its single number, thirty. She read it twice. He had selected the customer names and counted them, and he had used COUNT with the star, which she remembered from the library book had a specific behavior she had never fully believed until she tested it herself one night at the public library terminal.

"Run it again," she said. "But instead of the star, count the order ID column. The one from the Orders table."

Percy typed it. The number came back twenty-six. He stared at it. He counted the rows by hand on the screen, tapping each name with his finger, and got to four customers whose order column was empty, blank in every row the join had produced.

"They're the same join," Percy said. "I didn't change the join. I only changed what I counted."

"I know," Mackenzie said.

"Then which number is real?"

She pulled a stool over next to his. Behind them the door chimed and a woman came in holding a phone with a spiderweb crack across its face, diaphanous as frost on a window, and Mackenzie took it, wrote a ticket, told her ninety minutes, and came back. She did not sit down yet. She picked up the shop's demo tablet and a screen protector and began to suture the two together with the smoothing card, working the bubbles out from the center, because the morning's repairs did not pause for Percy's grade.

"Here's what I think happens," she said, working the card. "When you LEFT JOIN, a customer with no orders still gets a row. The row just gets filled in with NULLs where the order data would go. The row exists. It's one row."

"So counting rows counts them."

"COUNT with the star counts rows," she said. "So a customer with no orders gets counted once, because of that NULL-filled row. But if you count the order column itself, the column is empty, and you get zero for that customer." She set the tablet down. "That's why your thirty said everyone ordered. And why the twenty-six is the customers who actually did."

Percy looked at the screen for a long time. "So which one did the assignment want?"

"Both, probably. It depends what question you're asking. Do you want to know how many customers exist, or how many ordered?"

"That's not fair. Both questions sound the same out loud."

"They only sound the same until you decide what a customer with nothing counts as." She said it and then heard how it sounded, and Percy laughed, and she let it go. She went back to the counter, rang up a man buying a charging cable, and answered a call about a battery replacement. When she hung up, Percy had written both queries side by side and was running them over and over, thirty, twenty-six, thirty, twenty-six, like checking a door he knew was locked.

"My mom says computers are either right or wrong," he said. "She works at a dentist's office and thinks everything is like that, one answer, like a theocracy where there's a single truth and you just obey it. But this is two true answers that don't match."

Mackenzie finished with the screen protector and held the tablet up to the light to check her work. "Then the assignment is probably asking which truth you meant," she said. "Write down why you picked the one you picked."

Percy closed the Chromebook and stood, and at the door he turned around. "The four who never ordered. Should I feel bad for them?"

She hadn't thought about it. She looked at the ticket rack, at the cracked phone waiting in its sleeve with its promised ninety minutes, and said she didn't know, and Percy pushed through the door into the heat.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims who can afford it give a set charity called zakat al-fitr for each family member, so that poor families can also celebrate Eid.
story:
The cultural center smelled of cardamom and floor wax, and the folding tables along the back wall had been pushed together into one long surface covered with newspaper. Logan's father set a bag of rice beside the stack of dates and began counting small envelopes into piles, one for each member of the family. Tomorrow morning, before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, every one of those envelopes had to reach the collection box by the stage.

"Seven," his father said, laying the last envelope down. "You, your mother, me, your grandmother, the twins, and Amma." He tapped the seventh envelope twice, as if sealing an agreement with it. "Zakat al-fitr," he said, "for each of us."

Logan knew the phrase the way he knew the exits of his high school, without ever having to use the knowledge. What he hadn't known, until tonight, was that the amount was fixed, the same for every family that could afford it, and that the whole point of fixing it was so the envelopes in the box would add up to enough for poorer families to celebrate Eid too. His father had explained none of this. Logan had simply watched him count, and then asked a question, and the arithmetic had answered itself: the man who swept this building, whose kids went to school two blocks from Logan's, would have dates and rice tomorrow because of envelopes like these.

His father wanted the counting done correctly, that much was clear. He had been a banker in Karachi before they moved here, and he treated the night before Eid like a closing, sleeves rolled, receipts clipped. But Logan could see the second want underneath it. His father kept glancing at the door, and at his phone, waiting for Amma's son, Logan's uncle Farhan, who had not come to a family gathering in three years and had, an hour ago, texted a single word: coming.

Logan had his own preoccupations. In September he would start at a college two states away, and his mother had spent the evening amortizing the tuition over ten years of projected income, laying it out like a loan officer, steady payments, interest hidden in the decimals. She was not parsimonious by nature, but she had become so out of necessity, and lately Logan had begun to suspect that thrift was contagious, that he was catching it, that he would arrive on campus already middle-aged in his spending. His government teacher would have said the financial aid office was an oligarchy of five people who decided everything behind a closed door. Logan had laughed at that in class. Tonight, counting other people's money into envelopes, he wasn't laughing.

Here was the thing he could not settle. At school, charity was presented as a private virtue, a matter of personal conscience, and Logan had absorbed that version thoroughly: you gave because you chose to, and the choosing was what made it good. But what his father was doing tonight was not exactly choosing. The amount was set, the obligation fell on everyone who could afford it, and no one was praised for it because no one was supposed to be praised for it. It worked more like a tax that nobody collected and nobody evaded, or at least nobody in this room. Logan held both systems in his head, the voluntary one and the set one, and tried to see which he actually believed in. The voluntary one felt freer. The set one, he had to admit, fed more people.

The doors opened at half past nine. Uncle Farhan came in with a paper bag from the grocery store and the uncertain posture of a man testing ice. He set dates on the newspaper without a word, and Logan's father looked at the bag, then at his brother, then pulled an eighth envelope from the box.

"You're family," his father said. "That counts."

"I brought dates," Farhan said. "I thought it was a potluck."

"It's not a potluck. Sit down and help me count."

Logan watched them work side by side, his father narrating the arithmetic, Farhan nodding, neither of them mentioning the three years. Logan slipped the seventh envelope, the one with his name penciled on it in his father's handwriting, into the box by the stage. He was still not sure whether giving because you had to was worth less than giving because you wanted to. But the envelope was in the box, and tomorrow somebody's children would eat because of it, and Logan found that the uncertainty sat easier in him than it had an hour before, like a stone that had found the bottom of a full glass.

His mother called from the kitchen that the samosas were ready. Farhan stood first, and his father stood after him, and both of them went toward the smell of frying without deciding anything out loud.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: Canada's Rand formula, from Justice Ivan Rand's 1946 ruling after a Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario, requires all workers covered by a union contract to pay dues.
story:
The pay stub was thin paper, the kind that turned soft with sweat in a back pocket, and Lea read it twice under the fluorescent glare of the warehouse break room. Wages, overtime, and then a line she had never noticed before her eighteenth week of summer work: union dues, eleven dollars and change, taken off like tax. She had never joined anything. She had signed one form, the day she was hired, and a woman named Carol had checked her forklift certification and pointed her at aisle nine.

"You look like someone stole your lunch," said Marcus, dropping onto the bench across from her with his own stub held up to the light. He was twenty, quiet most of the time, with a scar on his forearm he never explained.

"Someone's taking money off my pay and I didn't sign up for it."

"It's called the Rand formula." He said it the way he said aisle numbers, flat, obvious. "Justice Ivan Rand, 1946. Came out of the Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario. Everyone covered by a union contract pays dues, whether they joined or not."

Lea turned the stub over as if the back might hold more. Outside the loading bay doors, trucks reversed in long beeps, and the dock plates clanged down one after another. "That doesn't seem fair," she said, and meant it, and also heard how young it came out.

Marcus shrugged. "Wage scale's fair. Overtime after forty-four hours is fair. You think this place gives that out of the goodness of its heart?" He tore the perforated edge off his stub and rolled it between his fingers. "My first year, before I understood anything, I resented it too. Then I watched the committee argue down the speed-up on the sort line, and it cost them three weeks of meetings after shifts, and they still showed up. I decided to internalize it differently. Dues are the price of the door staying open. Most of the time you don't see what the door is for."

The subtext sat between them, heavier than the words. Lea knew her mother had worked non-union at a laundry through her whole childhood, no pension, no wage scale, let go in a slow November with two weeks' pay and an apology that meant nothing. Her mother had put whatever she could into an annuity in those years, small deposits, disciplined ones, and she still called it the thing she was proudest of, because it was hers alone, because no committee had voted on it, because nobody could take it back. Two houses, two ways of thinking about what safety looked like. Lea had grown up inside the second one and was standing in the first.

She spent her lunch walking the long corridor to the union board, a corkboard thick with paper: minutes of meetings, a grievance about heat in the summer, the wage grid with its neat ascending rows, the shift premium, the safety clause about ventilation that someone had highlighted in yellow years ago. Carol was there tacking up a notice, and Lea asked her, half a question, whether the eleven dollars bought anything for someone who was leaving for university in September anyway.

"Your contract covers you while you're covered," Carol said. "That's all it promises. The rest is longer than you." She tapped the wage grid. "Kid before you, kid after you, same rows. You pay into the rows, you get the rows. You go, and it keeps going."

That night Lea sat on her bed with the stub flattened on her knee and thought about her mother's annuity statement, the tidy column of deposits, hers alone. The dues were the opposite kind of thing: money that went out into a common account she would never see itemized, spent partly on her, partly on strangers, partly on people not yet hired. Her mother would call that a bad bargain. Marcus would call it the only reason the bargain existed at all. Lea could not decide which was truer, and suspected the honest answer was equivocal, that the same deduction could be theft or inheritance depending on which month you looked at it.

In the morning she pinned the stub above her desk, next to the acceptance letter. At the end of her last shift, Marcus met her at the time clock with two coffees, and they drank them standing in the bay while the first truck of the night backed in, its beacon sweeping the concrete. "You never came to a meeting," he said. "I know," Lea said, and watched the dock plate fall.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under English common law, consideration must have some value but need not be a fair price; courts do not generally judge whether a bargain was a good one.
story:
The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and warm paper, and the air conditioning reached only the first three feet of the room, so Carter's collar was damp by the time he reached the teller line. He had forty dollars folded into his pocket, two twenties that had been one twenty until this morning, and a question he had been rehearsing since he left the house. Ahead of him a woman argued softly about a hold on a check, and the word liability drifted back over the velvet rope as though the bank itself were made of such words.

The teller who waved him forward was young, maybe twenty, with a name tag that said Priya and a lanyard heavy with pins. "Opening an account?" she asked. "Student checking takes ten minutes. You'll need to read the terms and conditions, and there's a signature card at the end. That's the consent part, basically. Your signature is you agreeing."

"I sold something," Carter said. "For twenty dollars. And I want to know if I can undo it."

Priya glanced at the queue behind him, three deep now, and lowered her voice. "Sold what?"

He told her about the bike, though telling it meant going back to yesterday evening, to the gravel drive beside Mr. Aldous's garage where the light had gone long and orange and the tire of the racing bike had spun slowly in his hand. Mr. Aldous had come out with his watering can, looked at the bike leaning against the fence, and said, "I'd give you twenty for that." Carter had needed twenty dollars. Not wanted, needed, by Friday, for the deposit on the cabin trip everyone had already paid, and the offer had seemed like a small synchronicity, the universe sliding the solution across the counter at the exact hour of his desperation. He had shaken on it right there, gravel gritting under his sneakers, the watering can dripping a dark coin of water onto the concrete.

"It's worth three hundred," Carter said now. "Maybe more. I checked online last night."

Priya pulled a blank deposit slip toward her and turned it over, as if the answer might be printed on the back. "Was it a fair price?" she asked, and when he shook his head she said, almost to herself, "Under common law, consideration just has to have some value. It doesn't have to be a fair price." She slid the slip back. "Courts don't sit around judging whether you made a good bargain. I'm doing law at night school, that's the only reason I know. Was it cash? Did you sign anything?"

"He wrote it on a napkin. From his porch. Both our names."

"Then it's signed."

The room seemed to tilt a little, the way it had in fourth grade when he learned that the sun would eventually swallow the earth, a fact too large to feel anything about in a carpeted building at eleven in the morning. Behind him a man cleared his throat. Priya's eyes went to a screen only she could see, some counter of accounts opened today, and Carter understood suddenly that she had a number to hit too, that everyone in the building was standing inside some bargain whose terms they had agreed to without reading, himself included. The whole morning had a turbid, stirred-up feeling, like the creek after rain, everything he thought was settled now moving in the water.

"Ten minutes for the account," Priya said. "It's a good one, no monthly fee if you keep a balance. And you should still go talk to him. He can undo a deal if he wants to, that's different from having to."

He opened the account because the twenty, folded and warm from his pocket, had nowhere else to live, and because the signature card waited with its empty line like a small door. He read the terms and conditions while Priya typed, the clauses rising off the page in a gray procession, liability limited, conditions subject to change, and he signed at the bottom and felt the pen drag slightly, leaving his name in blue ink, and thought of the napkin with both names on it in Mr. Aldous's careful draftsman's hand.

He walked home the long way, past the creek, and cut up Mr. Aldous's street without quite deciding to. The bike was there, leaning against the porch railing, polished, the chain oiled, the seat adjusted higher, which meant someone had ridden it already or meant to. Mr. Aldos came out with his watering can and saw him standing at the edge of the drive.

"I've been thinking about that price," Mr. Aldous said, and set the can down on the step.

"So have I," said Carter.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In 1824 German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past 'as it actually was', rather than to judge it or instruct the present.
story:
The essay question sat at the top of Addison's laptop screen like an accusation: Is it possible to describe the past without taking a side? She had come to her grandfather's house for the weekend because the internet at home was down, and because her mother had said, gently, that Grandpa could use the company.

The house was spartan since Grandma died, the spare furniture arranged as if for inspection, the study still crowded with boxes nobody had opened. Addison set up at the kitchen table while her grandfather washed the same pan he had washed before lunch. She had found the quote in her notes from class. In 1824, the German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past "as it actually was", rather than to judge it or instruct the present. Her job was to decide whether that was even possible.

"How's the paper?" her grandfather asked, drying his hands.

"Fine." She closed the laptop halfway. "Do you have any old letters? Like, from when you were young. Primary sources. My teacher wants primary sources."

He was quiet long enough that she thought he hadn't heard. "There's a box in the study. Your grandmother's side of the closet."

The study smelled of cedar and dust. Addison found the box under a stack of tax returns: bundled letters, a photograph album, a newspaper clipping from 1968 with a crease down the middle. She carried it to the kitchen table and began sorting, and her grandfather stood at the counter with his coffee, not quite watching, not quite not watching.

The clipping was about a student protest at his university. The article called the organizers "disruptive elements" and quoted the dean at length. There was no quote from any student. Addison turned the clipping over. On the back, in her grandmother's handwriting, was a single line: He was there. Ask him what he saw.

"Grandpa. This protest. Were you there?"

The coffee cup stopped halfway to his mouth. "That was a long time ago."

"That's not an answer."

He set the cup down. "I was there. It wasn't what the paper said."

She thought of a night three years ago, before Grandma got sick, when the two of them sat on the porch and Grandma told stories about her brother, the one nobody else mentioned, who had written pamphlets and lost his job for it and moved away. The family, Grandma said, had spent thirty years trying to exculpate themselves, as if his opinions were a crime they could prove they hadn't committed. Addison had looked up from the porch steps to see her grandfather standing inside the screen door, listening, saying nothing, going back to the dishes.

"The paper says the protest turned violent," she said now, tapping the clipping.

"The police turned it violent. Some kid threw a bottle, maybe. Then they waded in. I got pushed against a fence. A girl next to me got hit with a baton." He said it flatly, the way he said things that cost him. "The paper printed the dean's version. Nobody asked us."

Addison opened her laptop again. "So the newspaper is a primary source and you're a primary source, and they don't match."

"That happens."

"So which one do I believe? You're my grandfather. I want to believe you. Doesn't that mean I've already taken a side?"

He almost smiled. "Sounds like your paper's writing itself."

"It isn't." She pulled one of the letter bundles toward her. They were Grandma's letters to her sister, dated that same spring. Addison skimmed, stopped, read one twice. In it, Grandma described the protest, the fence, the baton, the girl, and one more thing: a list of names being circulated, students identified as organizers, and one of the names was her brother's, though the article had said nothing about any list. Addison looked up.

"There's a list in here that the newspaper never mentioned."

"Your grandmother kept everything." His voice had gone careful. "Even things that were dangerous to keep."

"That's why she wrote it down. Because the paper wasn't going to."

He sat down across from her, slowly, and for a while neither of them spoke. Outside, a mower started two houses away.

"So Ranke," Addison said, mostly to herself, and her grandfather raised an eyebrow. "This historian. He wanted to show the past as it actually was. No judging, no lessons for the present. Just what happened."

"The fence was real," her grandfather said. "The baton was real."

"But which things got written down, and which didn't, that's a choice somebody made. Even Grandma chose. She saved the clipping and the letter together, like she knew one wasn't enough."

She typed for a while, then stopped. "Here's my problem. If I only use the newspaper, I've taken the dean's side without meaning to. If I only use you and Grandma, I've taken yours. And if I use everything, somebody still decided what everything was."

"Then say that."

"Say what?"

"That you don't know for sure. That's what your grandmother would have said." He stood, took his cup to the sink, ran water over it. "She'd have made you put the clipping in the paper, though. Face up."

Addison flattened the crease with her thumb, then let it fold back along its old line. She set the clipping beside the letter, side by side on the table, and opened a fresh page.

"Can I copy the letter?" she asked. "The whole thing?"

"Take the box," he said, and turned off the tap.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface.
story:
Eric had promised himself he would finish the hallway drawing before fifth period ended, and he had forty minutes left, a pencil sharpened to a needle, and a hallway that refused to be a hallway. It lay on the paper like something flattened by a steamroller, a row of lockers marching across the page with the depth of a filing cabinet. He had drawn the drinking fountain three times. Each time it sat on top of the lockers instead of beside them, like a very clean frog.

"You've redrawn that fountain so many times it's going to ask for a contract," said Priya from the next stool, not looking up from her print of crows. She and Eric had a running arrangement: she critiqued his drawing, he critiqued her titles, and both of them ignored the teacher's suggestion that they critique their own work for once.

"The hallway's broken," Eric said. "It's a hallway for people with no depth perception. Flatland High School."

Priya leaned over, held her pencil at arm's length against his paper, and squinted like a pirate. "Everything's parallel. Your lockers are all the same size, and the door at the end is the same size too. That's why it looks like a poster for a very boring school."

He knew she was right, and he hated how right she was, because he had spent two nights on the tile pattern alone. The tiles. He had drawn a hundred tiles, each one exactly, obediently square, and somewhere in the back of his mind a suspicion had been forming that the tiles were the traitors. When he stood in the actual hallway, the far tiles looked smaller. He had never once drawn them smaller. He had, apparently, been running a hallway according to his own private laws of geometry, laws the hallway had never agreed to follow.

He flipped to a clean page and started over, this time being sneaky about it. He drew one point in the middle of the paper and then, feeling like a con artist, made the locker edges run toward that point like they were late for a bus. The tiles shrank as they went. The door at the end came out small, and strange, and then, all at once, deep. The hallway opened like a drawer sliding out of the page. He sat back so fast his stool squeaked.

"Whoa," Priya said. "What did you just do?"

"I don't know. I made the lines go toward one spot." He tapped the point with his eraser. "It's like everything's running away from the viewer to hide back there."

"That's a thing," Priya said, already pulling out her phone with the guilty speed of someone who knew the teacher would confiscate it in a heartbeat. "My brother did a report on it. Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective. Drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point, to show depth on a flat surface."

"So I accidentally invented it in an art room in Ohio."

"You're about six hundred years late and an ocean short, but sure, Columbus it however you like." She grinned. "Brunelleschi would be furious that you tried to expropriate his idea with a number two pencil."

"It's not expropriation if I didn't know it existed. It's independent rediscovery. It's very dignified."

The teacher drifted past, looked at the new drawing for a long moment, and said only, "Better," which from her was a standing ovation, and moved on. Eric looked at the vanishing point and felt both pleased and slightly cheated. He had wanted to invent something, and instead he had reinvented something, which meant either that he was six centuries late or that the idea was so true that a seventeen-year-old with a mechanical pencil could stumble into it on a Tuesday. He could not decide which of those he preferred, and the point itself, that small dot where the whole hallway went to disappear, gave him no help at all.

"Draw the drinking fountain now," Priya said. "It can finally live beside the lockers instead of on them, like a civilized amphibian."

Eric positioned his pencil, then paused. "One problem. If everything runs to the point, the fountain's edges have to aim there too, and it's off to the side. Do I give it its own point?"

"That's not a problem, that's Thursday."

He laughed, sharpened the pencil again, and began the fountain for the fourth time, angling its lines carefully toward that one small dot at the end of the hall.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
story:
Jessica's father tossed her the keys the way he might have tossed her a softball, underhand and unremarkable, and she caught them against her chest in the driveway while the June heat pressed down on the both of them. She had turned seventeen two weeks earlier, which meant she could finally predicate her independence on a piece of plastic from the DMV, but first she had to survive her father's teaching, and she knew from her cousin that this was no small thing. He had already reorganized the passenger seat three times, moving a water bottle, then a phone charger, then the water bottle back, as though the car's interior were a paragraph whose syntax had to be exactly right before anything could proceed.

"Seat, mirror, seatbelt," he said. "In that order, every time."

She adjusted the rearview mirror until the whole rear window sat inside its frame, then leaned sideways to fix the left mirror, and he watched without correcting her, which felt like a kind of applause. The engine started louder than she expected. She eased the car down the driveway with her foot hovering over the brake the way a pianist hovers over a wrong note, and they rolled out onto Farrow Street, where the speed limit was twenty-five and the maple branches made a shifting ceiling of light.

"The steering wheel isn't a suggestion," her father said after a hundred yards of small, anxious corrections. "You can commit."

So she committed, and the car straightened, and for three blocks she understood what everyone had been talking about. The whole street opened up in front of her. She could see the crosswalk ahead, the stop sign, the woman walking a dog, and she signaled for a right turn and took it wide, then tighter, and her father said "better," and she believed him.

They turned onto Miller Road, which had two lanes in each direction, and her father told her to get into the right lane for the turn at the pharmacy. She checked the right mirror. Empty road, silver and still in the afternoon glare. She put on the signal and began to drift over, and her father's hand came off his knee and pressed the wheel back toward its lane, and at the same moment a blue hatchback slid past on her right, close enough that she could see the driver's face, a college-aged guy mouthing something at her through his window.

"Whoa," she said, or something like it, her pulse in her ears. "I looked. I looked in the mirror."

"There's a spot the mirror can't cover," her father said. "Called a blind spot. You have to turn your head."

She pulled over at the pharmacy lot, her hands still shaped around the wheel, and turned her head to look at the space beside the car where the hatchback had been. Nothing there now, just hot asphalt and a shopping cart. "So even with the mirror," she said slowly, "there's an area I can't see at all. From the seat. No matter how I adjust it."

"That's why you turn your head before changing lanes," he said. "Mirror, then shoulder, then move."

She sat with that for a moment. It bothered her in a way she couldn't immediately name, and then she could: she had believed that seeing was mostly a matter of arranging the instruments correctly, the way she arranged her desk before studying, the way she built an essay's structure before writing a word of it. Arrange everything and the whole field would be visible. But the blind spot didn't care about arrangement. It was a permanent gap in the machine's perception, and the only remedy was for her to physically turn and look with her own eyes, to accept that no setup was complete.

"That guy was so close," she said, and heard her own voice come out petulant, which embarrassed her, so she straightened it out. "I'm sorry. I really thought the mirror was enough."

"He'll forget it by dinner," her father said. "You won't. That's the trade."

They did the pharmacy turn, then drove out to the old airport road where the traffic thinned to nothing, and she practiced the sequence until it became something other than thought: signal, mirror, shoulder, wheel. The first few times she overdid it, turning her whole torso and drifting in the lane, and her father laughed and said, "Your head, not your whole biography," and she laughed too, the sound startled out of her. By the fifth attempt she could glance over her shoulder and keep the car straight at the same time, and the glance had stopped feeling like an admission of failure and started feeling like what it actually was, a habit of humility built into the motion of driving.

Driving home, she caught herself wondering whether the mirrors could be positioned to shrink the blind spot, angled further outward, maybe, and whether her father's method was simply the old way of doing things. She asked him, and he shrugged and said some people did angle them differently, and that she could experiment when the car was hers. She liked that answer better than a lecture. She liked that there was a question left over, something she would have to work out with her own shoulders and her own mirrors, on her own roads, after he stopped riding beside her.

Back in the driveway, she parked crooked and had to try twice, and neither of them mentioned it. She cut the engine and sat with her hands on the wheel.

"Same time Thursday?" her father said.

"Same time Thursday," she said, and turned her head, out of pure habit now, to check the empty street behind her before she opened the door.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
The bleachers were spartan by the fourth quarter, cold metal gone soft with drizzle, and Hunter had stopped watching the game somewhere in the second. Beside him Wren pulled her sleeves down over her hands and said, "Do you want to get out of here?" and he said yes before he had decided to.

They walked to the coffee shop on Fenwick Street because it was the only place open, and for the first ten minutes it was fine, better than fine. She told him about the half-time show, the tuba player who had wandered off toward the concession stand and never come back, and he laughed in a way that surprised him. Then the story ended and nothing arrived to replace it, and the silence sat there like a third person at the table.

He remembered, then, the printout folded in his jacket pocket. His sister had emailed him a list that afternoon with a note he had read six times since: "Dad's on sabbatical, I'm in Vienna, you're on your own, so here. It worked on me and a stranger once, sort of. Love, Cass." The list was numbered one through thirty-six. At the top it said where it came from: a 1997 study by a man named Arthur Aron, where pairs of strangers took turns asking each other the questions, which grew gradually more personal, and ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk. He had stuffed it in his pocket thinking it might be a joke, or a lifeline, or both.

"I have something," he said, "and it's either going to be great or incredibly weird." He smoothed the paper flat between them. "In 1997, Arthur Aron ran a study. Pairs of strangers asked each other thirty-six questions, taking turns, and the questions get more personal as you go. They ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk." He looked up. "Do you want to try it?"

Wren read the first question with her chin propped on her fist. "When did you last sing to yourself?" she read. "Honestly? In the shower this morning. Badly." She laughed, and something in the room loosened. She answered too, something about the car, and then she read number two, and they were off, trading questions like cards, the answers starting small and getting stranger and truer as the numbers climbed.

Somewhere around question nineteen, his phone buzzed. Dex, from three rows back in the bleachers, presumably: "where'd you go. bonfire at peters after. you promised you'd come this time. i need you there man, gavin's bringing it up again and i want backup." Hunter read it twice. Dex had been his best friend since sixth grade, and Dex wanted him at that bonfire the way he had wanted things at seventeen, wholly and without complication, and Hunter understood that wanting, even admired it. He typed "can't tonight" and then deleted it and typed "later maybe" and put the phone face down, because some choices you make twice before you mean them.

"What's twenty?" Wren asked. He read it: If you were going to die suddenly, what would you most regret not having told anyone? She was quiet long enough that the espresso machine hissed and recovered. "I'd regret not telling my mom I'm not going to the college she picked," she said. "I told the other one yes without telling her. She finds out Monday." He asked what the other one was, and she said a art program, three states away, and he watched her say it like she was letting a bird out of a cage she'd built herself.

By question thirty-six they had been asked, in order, to name three things they liked about each other, and Hunter had managed two and stalled on the third, and Wren had said, "Take your time, it's the last one," and he had noticed how her whole attention felt like weather, warm and everywhere at once. He thought about how a list of questions could not really transmute strangers into anything, and yet here they were, two people who had known each other for three hours and seemed to know each other anyway, and he could not say which part was the questions and which part was her, and he suspected he would wonder about that for a long time.

"I don't know if this was the study or just you," he said finally, "but the third thing is, you ask questions like you actually want the answers."

Outside the window the stadium lights went dark, the game over, everyone spilling toward cars and bonfires. Wren folded the paper along its worn creases and slid it across the table to him. "Question thirty-seven," she said. "Same time next Friday?"

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2013 study by Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation.
story:
The new machines arrived on a Tuesday, four of them in shrink-wrapped pallets, and by Thursday they stood in a row where the magazine rack used to be. Jasmine watched the installers feed cables through the ceiling tiles while she bagged cereal and cold medicine at register three, the only human lane left open. Her manager, Denny, said they were "a pilot program," the way he said everything, like the words had been handed to him on a card.

That night the group chat lit up. It was called Saturday Shift Buddies, though nobody had worked a true Saturday together since spring. Priya posted a photo of the machines taken from behind the bakery case, and beneath it she wrote, "so are we all getting fired or."

Rafael, who worked at the library branch two blocks over and considered himself the chat's intellectual, replied first. "this is exactly that study. 2013, Frey and Osborne. they estimated 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation." Jasmine read it twice in her dark kitchen, phone held above her face. Forty-seven percent felt too big to be real and too specific to be made up.

She looked it up before she answered, because Rafael had a habit of being confidently approximate. He had it right, though. Two Oxford researchers, 2013, 47 percent. She typed, "you actually got one right for once," then deleted it, because Rafael had also been the one who told her the machines' cameras could flag the bakery case, and she wasn't ready to make that a joke yet.

What bothered her wasn't the number. It was the scheduling app the store had rolled out the same week, which had quietly rearranged everyone's hours according to something called a labor-optimization model. Priya's hours had been cut to nine a week. Jasmine's had not. When she asked Denny why, he shrugged and said the app balanced coverage against "engagement metrics," and that Jasmine's metrics were strong. She did not know what an engagement metric was, and she suspected Denny didn't either. It felt less like a manager deciding things and more like a contrivance that extruded decisions from somewhere no one could question, the same way the machines extruded receipts, thin and curled and slightly warm.

Saturday she worked the lane beside the new self-checkout row, which meant she was the one the machines summoned when they got confused. "Unexpected item in the bagging area," the voice would say, serene and feminine, and Jasmine would come press her code and watch the camera light blink at whatever the system had flagged. Around two o'clock it flagged Mr. Okafor, who came in every Saturday for bread and a lottery ticket and had never once set off anything. She cleared the alert and found herself standing there longer than the moment needed, watching the little red light go out.

In the chat that night she wrote, "the machines flagged mr okafor today. it's flagged him three times now. it has never flagged me once." Priya responded with a single eye emoji. Rafael wrote a paragraph about training data that she mostly skipped, and then, at the bottom, "honestly the app is weird too. it cut my hours and my engagement is fine. i checked."

Jasmine sat with the two things side by side: the machines that were coming, whatever the study said about 47 percent, and the systems already here, deciding whose hours mattered, who got watched. She didn't think they were the same problem, exactly, but she couldn't fully pull them apart either, and she was tired of pretending she could. She typed, "i don't know if the machines are the problem or if we're the problem for building them this way. maybe both. maybe we find out which." Then she added, "priya, i'm giving you two of my shifts until the app fixes itself. if it fixes itself."

Priya replied with three hearts and "you're literally the only non-hedonistic person in this chat," which made no sense to Jasmine until she remembered Priya had spent the summer reading philosophy for fun.

The twist came Monday, in the break room, where Jasmine found a printed memo taped inside the cabinet door. The pilot program had been proposed to the regional office eight months earlier, before any machines were ordered, by an employee suggestion program with a five-hundred-dollar bonus attached. The winning suggestion had a name on it. It was Priya's.

Jasmine photographed the memo, put her phone away, and stood in the little room with its vending machine and its clock that ran four minutes fast, holding both of Priyas at once: the one whose hours the app had starved, and the one who had, for five hundred dollars, helped design the hunger. She walked back out to register three, and the self-checkout voice greeted a customer, and the light above lane four began to blink.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, including those who already have hypertension.
story:
The waiting room had one wall of windows and a rack of pamphlets, and Jordan stood in front of it like a man choosing a career. He had agreed, two weeks earlier, to train as a peer health educator for the sophomore wellness class, and Ms. Adeyemi had told him to show up at the clinic on Thursday to practice with real materials before he stood in front of thirty fifteen-year-olds. The rack offered him laminated options: contraception, condom use, STI testing, consent. He took one of each and sat down beside his mother, who was folding and unfolding the appointment slip.

"You're staring at those like they're final exams," she said.

"They kind of are." He spread the pamphlets across his knee. "I have to explain this stuff to people my age. Out loud. In a room." What he did not say was that the health class at his school had spent exactly one period on any of it, a period in which the teacher read a slide in a monotone and the boys in the back laughed at the word condom, and that Jordan suspected half of what he'd absorbed came from the internet, in pieces, some of it wrong. Ms. Adeyemi had used the phrase "media hegemony" about online misinformation, the way certain voices dominate a subject until everyone else just repeats them, and Jordan had written it down because he wanted to be the voice that interrupted.

When the nurse called his mother's name, Jordan gathered the pamphlets and followed her back. His mother sat on the crinkling paper of the exam table while the cuff tightened around her arm, and the nurse looked at the number on the screen and looked at it again.

"It's a little high today," the nurse said. "Not an emergency. But let's have the doctor talk with you."

The doctor came in with a laptop and a unhurried manner, and she asked about salt, sleep, stress, and then exercise, and his mother said, honestly, that she drove to work, sat at work, and drove home. "The good news," the doctor said, "is that regular aerobic exercise, like brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, including people who already have hypertension." She turned the screen so they could see the number. "Most days. Not weekends of heroics. Consistency."

"Hypertension," his mother repeated, tasting the word like something she'd been accused of.

"High blood pressure," the doctor said. "That's the name for it."

While his mother made small talk with the doctor about her sister's heart pills, Jordan sat by the window and worked something out on the back of a pamphlet. He wrote brisk walking, most days, then drew seven boxes and began filling them: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, a gap on Thursday for his training, Thursday again, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. When the doctor left, he showed his mother the boxes. "There's a loop through the park behind the school," he said. "It's about a mile. If I come home and we walk it before dinner, that's most days right there. I'll be coming back from practice anyway."

"You want to walk with your old mother," she said, but she was looking at the boxes, and her finger touched the Thursday gap. "You can miss a day," she said. "Most days isn't every day."

"That's what the doctor said. Exactly that." He folded the paper and put it in his jacket, and it occurred to him that this was the first fact he'd collected all morning that he actually trusted, because it had come with a number on a screen and a doctor's unhurried voice and not from a comment section.

The practice session with Nurse Practitioner Okafor happened in a small consult room with two chairs and a box of sample kits. She played a sixteen-year-old named Sam who wanted to know things, and Jordan, sweating through his shirt, explained condoms and the pill and the ring and the shot, stumbling only when he got the effectiveness numbers tangled, and Okafor corrected him with a look rather than a lecture. Then she asked the hard one. "Say Sam didn't want to stop and the other person did. What do you tell Sam?"

Jordan was quiet long enough that the clock on the wall became loud. "Consent isn't a form you get signed once," he said finally. "It's continuous. You check in, you pay attention, and silence or freezing isn't a yes. And if you're unsure whether you have a yes, you stop and ask, because being profligate with someone's trust is worse than an awkward pause." He hadn't planned the sentence; it arrived whole, and Okafor nodded once, which felt like being handed a diploma.

"Testing," she said. "Sam asks where."

"Here, or the county clinic. It's confidential. You can walk in, ask to be tested for infections, and they take a urine sample or a blood draw depending on what they're screening for. Results come back in about a week, and if anything shows up, most of it's treatable." He'd rehearsed this part in the shower that morning, externalize the fear, his brother had told him once, meaning put it outside yourself where you can look at it, and it had worked: the sentences came out level.

Walking out through the waiting room, pamphlets under his arm, Jordan saw his mother still at the front desk scheduling her follow-up. He held up the folded paper with the seven boxes. "Monday," he said. "The park loop. Six o'clock."

"Six," she said. "Bring a jacket."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first to use video assistant referees, who can review goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity.
story:
The living room smelled of burnt popcorn and ceiling fan dust, and Nathaniel had the good seat, the corner of the couch, because he'd claimed it an hour before kickoff. His father stood behind him with a beer he wasn't drinking. Uncle Ray occupied the armchair like a garrison, already reddening at the collar, and Priya from next door sat cross-legged on the rug with her phone dark in her lap, which for Priya was a form of reverence.

It was the France match, or maybe the one after; the summer had blurred them together. What mattered was the ninety-first minute, a cross swung in, a scramble, the ball bulging the net, and then the whole room erupting and then going quiet in the same breath, because the referee had stopped, hand to his ear, staring at nothing, and the scoreboard said the goal was under review.

"No," his father said. "No, no. Not this."

"It's the VAR," Priya said, not looking up. "Video assistant referee."

"I know what it is." His father's voice had a cauterized flatness to it, as if the argument had already been burned shut for him somewhere else, in some earlier summer. "It's television deciding football. It's a lab experiment deciding football."

Uncle Ray heaved himself forward, choleric and delighted, veins mapping his temples. "It's justice deciding football. You want chicanery rewarded? You want divers lifting trophies? You saw the replay. That was a shove. I've seen it, you've seen it, the whole world's seen it."

"The whole world's seen it four times from four angles, that's the problem." His father set the beer down on the shelf with a click. "Football used to be one angle. One ref, one truth, one moment, and you lived with it. You argued about it at dinner for thirty years. That was the game."

Nathaniel had been quiet through all of it, watching the screen where the referee stood with his finger to his ear like a man waiting on a verdict of his own. Earlier that month, before the knockout rounds, he'd looked it up himself, mostly to win an argument with Priya, and had found less ammunition than he expected. This World Cup in Russia was the first one to use the video assistant referees at all, the first tournament where a goal could be pulled back like this, and it wasn't only goals they could review, it was penalties and direct red cards and one strange thing he'd read twice to be sure: cases of mistaken identity, where the referee had booked the wrong man entirely. He'd laughed at that, alone at the kitchen counter. A whole system built partly for the sake of some poor right back who'd been shown a card meant for someone else.

On the rug, Priya turned to face the couch. "You're the one who wants it gone, Mr. Okafor. Tell him about 'sixty-six."

"Don't," his father said.

"He wasn't born yet. There's no footage. He thinks football was perfect before TV ruined it."

"There was a goal that maybe wasn't a goal, or maybe was, in a year before your parents met," his father said, to Nathaniel, "and men in my family have argued about it at every wedding and funeral since. That argument is a possession. VAR wants to take it away from us and give us a fact instead."

"That's the most sentimental thing I've ever heard," Uncle Ray said. "You'd rather be robbed beautifully than paid correctly."

"Sometimes, yes. Obviously yes."

The room laughed, even Priya, but Nathaniel didn't, because he was realizing something and wanted to finish realizing it before the screen resolved. His father wasn't only being nostalgic; he was defending the argument itself, the long family row, the pleasure of an unprovable case. And Uncle Ray wasn't only being stubborn; he'd watched too many cheats get away with it, and a machine that saw truly was, to him, a kind of mercy. Both of them were right about something, and both of them wanted him to choose, and the referee on the screen still hadn't chosen either.

Nathaniel thought: I don't have to pick a side of the room. He could hold both, the beauty of doubt and the decency of getting it right, and admit he didn't yet know where the seam between them ran, or whether justice and romance could share a sport. He opened his mouth to say some version of that, something careful, something that would honor his father without abandoning Ray.

The screen flashed. The referee drew a square in the air with both hands, sharp and small, like locking a door. Goal disallowed. Uncle Ray roared. His father sat down for the first time all night, slowly, next to Nathaniel, and said nothing. Priya reached over and turned the volume up.

"You still watching?" she asked.

"Every frame," Nathaniel said.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel.
story:
The metronome had belonged to Christopher's grandfather, a pyramid of walnut with a brass pendulum that swung behind a slit in the case, and after the funeral his mother set it on the piano at home where nobody played. Christopher found it again the night before his audition for the jazz ensemble, when he was trying to count through a passage in the sheet music and losing his place each time. He wound the key, set the sliding weight to 120, and let the ticking fill the living room. His father came to the doorway with his coat still on.

"Who invented that thing?" Christopher asked.

"Some German, I think. Look it up if you care." His father hung his coat and went to the kitchen.

Christopher cared. He cared because he had told Mr. Reyes, the band director, that he would audition Thursday after school on the baritone saxophone, an instrument he had been teaching himself since September from a photocopiated method book with someone else's pencil marks in the margins. Most of the saxophones at Lincoln High belonged to the school. The baritone, dented along its bell like a car that had been in a mild accident, belonged to the school too, and Mr. Reyes had made it clear that keeping it out meant proving he could actually play it.

He looked up the metronome on his phone while the pendulum ticked. Johann Maelzel had patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel. He said the names out loud once, quietly, so they would stick. Maelzel took the patent; Winkel had the design first. He sat with that for a while, the ticking going on beside him, before he transcribed the tempo marking from his sheet music onto a sticky note and pressed it to the piano's music stand.

The band room on Thursday smelled of valve oil and floor wax. Mr. Reyes was writing something at his desk, and Priya Nair, a senior who ran the saxophone section, was taking chairs down off the stacks because the janitor had complained about it at the last rehearsal. Christopher assembled the baritone, and the instrument went together with a clunk he felt in his teeth.

"Play the etude from the top," Mr. Reyes said, not looking up. "Don't stop."

He stopped four times in the first eight bars. His fingers knew where to go at home, at 100 beats a minute, patient and forgiving. At the tempo the etude demanded they went somewhere else, somewhere his ears could not follow. Mr. Reyes finally set down his pen.

"You're practicing slow and playing fast. That's like studying French and then taking the test in German."

"My grandfather had a metronome," Christopher said. "I was using it last night."

"Then use it right." Mr. Reyes pulled out his phone, opened a tuner app with a click track, and set it on the stand. "Sixty. One note per click. I don't care if it sounds terrible. I care that it's even."

Priya had stopped arranging chairs. Christopher played. Sixty was so slow it felt like a different piece of music, each note hanging alone in the wax-smelling air, and the temptation to rush came up in him like a physical thing, an itch in his wrists. He held it. On the third line he heard something he had never heard at home, a small gap between his third and fourth fingers that had been hiding inside the faster tempo for months.

Later, in the hallway, Priya caught up with him. "He failed me at that audition two years ago," she said. "Then he let me in anyway."

"So which is it? Did he fail you or not?"

"Both, kind of. I was bad, and he thought I'd keep going." She shouldered her backpack. "He told my mom I was sagacious about practicing. He means it as a compliment, I think. It's a word he saves for people."

Christopher got home before his father did.
