The walnut metronome sat on the piano where his mother had left it, and he wound the key again, set the weight low, and played along with the grandfather's machine at a speed no performance would ever demand. It was Maelzel's name on the patent, he thought, but Winkel's design underneath, and nobody at the audition would ever know which of the two had made the click in this room. He thought about Mr. Reyes, who had failed Priya and passed her in the same breath. Both, kind of.

He did not know yet whether he had passed. He would find out Monday, at rehearsal, by whether there was a chair set out for the baritone or not, and he understood that he would not be told, exactly, but shown. His phone buzzed against the piano. Priya: "He keeps a list on his desk. Yellow legal pad. Don't ask how I know."

Christopher set the phone face down, counted four clicks of the swinging brass pendulum, and lifted the horn.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Eye-contact norms differ: steady eye contact often signals confidence in North American interviews, while in some East Asian settings prolonged direct gaze at a senior person can seem impolite.
story:
Justin sat on the swing at the far end of the playground, knees apart, a folded copy of his application in one hand. His cousin Dara stood in the wood chips in front of him holding a printed list of questions and a phone to record the time. The job was at the garden center by the river, twenty hours a week, and the interview was Monday.

"Question one," Dara read. "Tell me about yourself."

"I'm Justin, I just graduated, I worked the cash register at my uncle's store, I can lift fifty pounds." He said it to the fence behind Dara's head.

"That's the answer your dad made you memorize," Dara said. "Look at me when you say it. You're interviewing with the manager, not the fence."

That was the problem, and both of them knew it before anyone said it out loud. His father had drilled him for two evenings in the kitchen: steady eye contact, hold it through the answer, that's what confidence looks like in an interview here. Then his grandmother had watched one of the practice sessions from the doorway, and when he held his father's gaze for a full question and answer she had remonstrated with him, sharp and quiet at the same time, saying that staring straight at a senior person that long was rude, that a young man should lower his eyes and show respect. His father said she was talking about the old country. She said he was talking about television. Justin had gone to bed with both instructions in his head and no way to follow them at once.

He tried it now. He looked at Dara's eyes and began the answer again, and four words in he dropped his gaze to the wood chips, then dragged it back up, then away again. Dara stopped the timer.

"You look like you're flinching."

"I'm not flinching. I'm deciding."

"Decide before Monday."

He stood up off the swing and walked to the water fountain by the slide, which had been dry since spring, and pressed the button anyway out of habit. He was thinking about which of them was actually right, and he noticed he had been framing it that way, as though one of them had to be wrong. But his grandmother had spent forty years in offices in Seoul before she retired here, and his father had been interviewing and hiring people in this city for fifteen. It was possible they were both describing something real, in different rooms, and the difference was the rooms.

"Ask me the question again," he called back. "Don't tell me when you're going to."

Dara folded his arms. "Tell me about yourself."

Justin walked back toward him and answered the whole thing, forty seconds, watching Dara's face the entire time, and this time it held, because he had stopped trying to do both things at once and had chosen. The manager at the garden center was local. Her name was on the email, a name like half the names in his graduating class. Whatever was true of prolonged gaze in a room in Seoul, this interview was in the room it was in, and Justin decided he would meet her eyes and not count the seconds while he did it.

"I don't know if it's respectful," he said. "I don't actually know what she'll think. Maybe she'll find it too much."

"Too much?"

"Some people do. That's the part I can't know from here." He picked the application off the swing and folded it along its original creases. The paper had his grandmother's handwriting in the margin from the night she'd watched, three small characters he couldn't read, next to the line about customer service. He had assumed she was correcting him. Now he looked at it longer and thought she might have been correcting his father.

The afternoon was cooling and the playground had emptied except for a man reading on a bench near the riparian walk that ran behind the equipment, the strip of mown grass between the fence and the river. The days after graduation had felt like an interregnum, school over and the job not yet begun, and Justin had been filling them with forms and practice and this swing. He put the application in his back pocket.

"Monday, ten o'clock," Dara said, gathering the list of questions. "You want one more run-through?"

"One more," Justin said, and sat back down on the swing. "Ask me why I want to work at a garden center."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
story:
The driving school car was waiting at the end of the driveway when Lauren came out, a small silver thing with a fat yellow L stuck to its back. Her mother stood at the front step with her arms crossed, not quite on the porch and not quite in the yard, the way she stood at school concerts, at the edge of whatever was happening. The car had no gearstick between the seats. Lauren had chosen the automatic lessons two months ago, ticking the box on the form in the kitchen while her mother read the letter from the insurance company, and neither of them had said anything about it since.

"Ready?" the instructor asked. His name was Dev, and he had a clipboard he never looked at.

"Nearly." Lauren had the provisional licence in her hand and a reason in her head that she hadn't yet said aloud: the automatic was easier, and she wanted the test passed by September, before term started. The family car, the old green hatchback her mother drove to the hospital three mornings a week, had a gearstick and three pedals, and it sat in the driveway behind them now like a fact she was trying to park behind her.

She settled into the driver's seat, adjusted the mirror, and found the pedal layout strange in a way she couldn't name at first. Two pedals, not three. Her left foot had nothing to do, so it hovered, then pressed itself flat against the floor as if it could be subsumed there, folded away like a third option nobody had wanted.

They drove. Dev talked her out of the close and onto the ring road, and the car moved when she asked it to and stopped when she asked it to, without argument, without the clutch-work she'd watched her mother perform for eighteen years, heel rocking, hand dropping to the stick at every corner. It felt almost munificent, the way it gave her motion for so little in return. She said so, and Dev laughed and said that was one way of putting it.

It was at the roundabout, waiting, that she said the thing. "If I pass in this, can I drive our car? It's a manual." Dev shook his head, eyes still on the traffic. "Pass in an automatic, you can drive automatics, full stop. You'd have to pass again, in a manual, before you could drive one." Lauren sat with that while the car in front moved and she moved after it. So the choice she'd made in the kitchen wasn't a choice about lessons at all. It was a choice about which genus of driver she'd be licensed as, and she'd made it in thirty seconds, with a biro, over toast. Her mother needed the hospital on Tuesdays. On Thursdays, when the early shift ran, somebody had to be able to take the car.

They did hill starts on a quiet street, although in this car a hill start was only a matter of holding the brake, and Lauren found herself inventing difficulty where there was none, pretending the pedal arrangement was a smaller version of the whole problem. She asked Dev about manual lessons, prices, whether he taught both. He said he did, and that they could switch next week if she wanted, and that she was further along than most learners at hour one, which she suspected he said to everyone, and which helped anyway.

Back at the house, the silver car pulled in behind the green one, and her mother came down the drive with her cardigan buttoned wrong at the bottom, one eye on the clipboard man as if he were a health visitor. Lauren sat with the engine off and didn't get out. She was eighteen; she could sign herself up for either test and pay for it with the birthday money her grandmother had been, as always, quietly munificent about. But the easy road had a fence at the end of it, and she'd only just now been shown the gate. She looked at the gearstick of the family car through the windscreen, the little worn knob of it, and thought of her mother's hand going to it without looking, the way you'd touch something that lived with you.

Her mother tapped the window with one knuckle. Lauren lowered it.

"Well?" her mother said. "How was it?"

Lauren looked past her at the green car, and put the handbrake on, though it was already on. "Can you drive me to the shops tomorrow?" she said. "I want to watch your feet."

fact: White coat hypertension is when blood pressure reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, so doctors may check it with home or all-day monitoring.
story:
The cuff hissed, and Parker counted the ticks as the needle settled, the way the nurse had shown him in the hospital room two weeks after his father came home. His father sat at the kitchen table with his sleeve rolled up, reading the sports section, his forearm dusted with the fine gray hair that Parker somehow had never noticed before. One fortyy-six over ninety. Parker wrote it in the notebook, then slid the notebook out of sight when his father glanced over.

The first number had been higher. At the follow-up appointment on Tuesday, the machine in the exam room had flashed something in the sixteens over the high nineties, and Parker had watched his father's face go still and formal, the way it did at funerals. But the doctor had only leaned back on his stool and asked, before prescribing anything, whether they could measure at home instead. "Sometimes it reads high just from being in here," she said. "It's called white coat hypertension." Then she'd handed Parker a cuff and a pamphlet, as if he were the patient's secretary rather than his son.

Parker had spent three evenings with the pamphlet and then with the laptop, past his old habit of stopping at the first result. He learned that the top number was the pressure when the heart pushed, the bottom when it rested, and that the numbers answered to slow things: salt pulling water into the blood, walking widening the vessels over time, weight easing the work of the pump. It was less like chemistry than like argument. Everything negotiated. Nothing decided in a single reading.

His father had spent thirty years deciding otherwise. Parker remembered the summers his father had driven to job sites on two hours of sleep, the birthday he'd waved off chest pain as "garbage from the drive-through," the capricious way he'd take the stairs one month and refuse them the next. Now he was supposed to convalesce, a word the discharge papers used and nobody in the house said aloud, and he treated it as a foreign occupation, some temporary hegemony of doctors and pill organizers that would eventually be overthrown.

"Dad. Arm."

His father folded the paper. "You're enjoying this."

"Somebody has to write the numbers down." Parker wrapped the cuff, aligned the marker over the artery the way the diagram showed, and pressed the button. While the machine inflated, his father studied the window over the sink, where the tomato plants had gone leggy and brown. When it finished, the screen read one thirty-two over eighty-four.

"Better," Parker said, and logged it, and then sat back. Better than Tuesday at the hospital, anyway. But Thursday it had been one thirty-eight, and Saturday morning, after pancakes, one fortyy-two, and he still couldn't say which of those was the real one, or whether the real one was a single thing at all. The doctor had said she'd want a fuller picture before deciding about medicine, maybe even a monitor that read all day, and Parker understood now that she wasn't being cautious. She was refusing to let one frightened number in one bright room speak for his father's whole life.

"So what's it mean," his father said. It wasn't really a question. He was looking at the notebook now, at the column of figures in Parker's careful print.

"It means the machine at the clinic was scared of you." Parker tapped the page. "Here, at home, you're lower. Not perfect. The walk Dr. Reyes wants you doing, the salt thing, that's what moves it over weeks. It doesn't jump in a day."

His father was quiet long enough that Parker heard the refrigerator cycle on, a low hum under the room. Parker thought of asking him, finally, about those years of drive-throughs and skipped physicals, whether he'd known, whether knowing would have changed anything. He didn't ask. He wasn't sure he wanted the answer more than he wanted the afternoon.

"We walking tonight or not?" his father said. He rolled his sleeve down, but slowly, and left the paper folded on the table.

Parker closed the notebook. "After dinner. And I'm cooking."

"No salt."

"Some salt," Parker said, and got up to see what was left in the crisper.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf and menu prices usually do not include sales tax, which is added at the register, so the total is higher than the posted price.
story:
Gabrielle counted the bills twice on the bus, the way her mother counted rent money, pressing each one flat against her knee. Sixty-two dollars and some coins, her first paycheque cashed at the pharmacy counter because the bank wanted two pieces of ID she didn't have yet. She had worked eleven hours at the hardware store over two Saturdays, sweeping, stacking, and fetching paint cans from the back. Eleven hours at nine dollars an hour, she had calculated on her phone three times, came to ninety-nine dollars. The envelope in her pocket held sixty-two. Somewhere between those numbers, thirty-seven dollars had vanished, and she intended to find out where.

The pay stub was folded into quarters in her back pocket, and she smoothed it open on the counter before Mr. Okafor arrived to unlock the doors. The print was small and merciless. Gross pay, it said, $99.00, which was her number, her hours, her broom calluses. Below it a column of subtractions: Federal income tax. State income tax. FICA, which she said aloud once, "fica," like a word in a language she didn't speak. Net pay, $62.41. She had heard her father complain about deductions at dinner, half-listening, the way she half-listened to weather reports, but the words had seemed to belong to a country she wouldn't visit for years. Apparently she had arrived. She was still staring at the stub when Danny from the paint counter leaned over her shoulder.

"Welcome to being employed," he said. "You pay them for the privilege." He was twenty, saving for a motorcycle he described in terms normally reserved for geology, all gleaming surfaces and deep internal structure, the whole machine igneous to him somehow, born of fire. He tapped the FICA line. "That one follows you forever."

"Nine dollars an hour," Gabrielle said slowly, "is not nine dollars an hour."

"Danny's tax literacy hour," someone called from the stockroom, and Danny raised his coffee mug in acknowledgment, unbothered.

By noon her feet ached and she had developed a private catalogue of the store's customers: the ones who read labels, the ones who didn't, the ones who brought items to the register without prices and watched her wait for a price check as though she were personally responsible for the mystery. At her register, which she was allowed to use when Lorna took lunch, she noticed something else. A woman bought a drill marked $39.99 and paid $43.19. A boy maybe a year older than Gabrielle bought tape and sandpaper and counted out coins that were somehow not enough. "There's tax," Lorna told him, not unkindly, waving him toward the ATM in the corner with an expression that suggested this happened all day, every day, a small recurring theatre of surprise.

Gabrielle thought about her own money, the sixty-two, and about the prom dress folded in its bag at home, which she had found at the thrift store for twenty dollars, a colour like a summer storm. Her friend Priya had declared they would go for pho afterwards, the two of them, a cheap celebration, and the menu said the large bowl was $12.95. Gabrielle had thirteen dollars left after the dress, exactly enough, she had figured on the bus. She looked at the register, at the drill receipt still curled in the tray, and felt the ground shift a little, the way it did in math class when a proof turned out to depend on something she'd assumed was solid and wasn't.

At three, during her break, she did the arithmetic on a paint swatch card, deep teal, on the blank side. She had learned, by watching, that posted prices were not totals. The menu said $12.95 but the register would add the tax on top, and the total would come to more than the price taped to the wall. She wrote 13.00 and crossed it out. Wrote 14.00 and put a question mark beside it. The bus was $2.50 each way. She looked at the numbers until they stopped being numbers and became the shape of a decision.

Here is what she had believed, or half-believed, that morning: that taxes were simply removed from you, a door that shut, money that went into a dark building somewhere and did not return. That was one way of seeing it, her father's way, the way that made paying sound like being robbed politely. But the stub in her pocket told a more complicated story, and the boy at the register with his insufficient coins told another. The sales tax had surprised him; her income tax had surprised her; and yet the road she'd taken the bus on had been paved, and the school she'd graduate from in June was free to her, and somebody had paid for those, possibly in small infuriating letters, FICA, FICA, FICA, all the way down. It wasn't that she'd decided taxes were good. It was that she'd decided the sentence "taxes are bad" was the kind of sentence that couldn't be true all the way through, like saying rain was bad, which it was, if you had somewhere to be, and wasn't, if you were a reservoir. She could hold both. What she couldn't yet see was where the money actually went, in what proportions, and she suspected the not-knowing was the part her father actually hated. She wrote on the swatch card, in tiny letters, look it up, and put it in her pocket next to the stub.

After work she took the bus to the pho place and got there before Priya. She read the menu board again, the prices clean and confident, and thought about how the numbers there were promises that stopped at the register. She counted her money once more. Then she took out her phone and moved eight dollars from her savings envelope, the one labelled in her own handwriting EMERGENCIES, into her wallet, and did not feel great about it, and did not feel terrible either. When Priya arrived, dropping into the chair with her backpack still on, Gabrielle slid the menu across.

"Order whatever," she said. "I've got a buffer."

"A buffer."

"I did math today," Gabrielle said. "Real math. Angry math." She pointed at the board. "The twelve-ninety-five is a lie, by the way. Not the whole price. You find out at the register." Priya looked at her for a second, then laughed, and reached for a menu.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
The restaurant smelled like onions and floor bleach, and the manager, a woman named Dot with a pen tucked behind each ear, slid a clipboard across the granite countertop before Andrew had even sat down. "Paperwork first," she said. "Then aprons."

The form was stapled to a packet, and at the top it said Form I-9. He had expected a W-4, because his cousin had told him about the W-4, taxes withheld, boxes for dependents, all of it boring but familiar in shape. This was different. It asked whether he was a citizen, a lawful permanent resident, an alien authorized to work, and it wanted him to swear under penalty of perjury that everything he wrote was true. He read the small print twice, and there it was, plain as a bus schedule: every new employee must complete Section 1, which verified identity and permission to work, no later than the first day of paid work. Today was, according to the schedule taped to the fridge, his first day of paid work. Four to nine, bussing tables.

"I need my passport," Andrew said. "Or my birth certificate. I didn't bring it."

Dot pulled the pen from her left ear and tapped the schedule. "You start in," she checked her watch, "forty minutes."

"I live eight minutes away. Six if I run." He was already standing. His father had dropped him off and gone to the hardware store, and his father's phone, when Andrew called from the counter, rang and rang and went to voicemail. His mother was at her shift at the clinic. The passport, he suddenly remembered, was not in the fireproof box under his parents' bed where it belonged. It was in his mother's desk drawer, because she had needed it in March to renew something, and his mother was a woman who filed things according to the pragmatics of the moment rather than any system she could later reconstruct.

"Go," Dot said. "But if you're not back by four, I have to send you home. I can't put you on the clock without it."

He ran. The afternoon had that hard late-summer light that makes every lawn look like a photograph of itself, and he cut through the Hendersons' yard and the gap in the fence by the drainage ditch, where somebody had dumped a chunk of black rock, glossy and speckled, some kind of igneous thing a geology teacher would have identified in a second. Andrew had taken that class last spring. He had liked it, the idea that the same planet could produce granite and pumice and obsidian out of the same raw heat, depending on how it cooled. Everything depended on the conditions. His father said that about people too, usually when defending somebody Andrew thought was indefensible.

The house key was under the mat. The desk drawer yielded the passport on the second try, wedged beneath a folder of insurance papers, and he stood for a second in the silent kitchen holding it, out of breath, before running back. In the car his father would have said, you should have checked the requirements beforehand, and he would have been right, and it would also have been useless, the way true things could be useless. Andrew had checked whether he needed working papers from the school, because that was what the internet forums said. No one had mentioned this form. There was a difference between being careless and being uninformed, and he intended to hold on to that difference, though he could feel it thinning as he ran.

He came through the restaurant door at 3:52, sweating through his shirt, and Dot looked at the clock and then at him and said nothing, which was somehow worse than a speech. He sat at the granite counter and filled out Section 1 in block letters, checked the citizen box, signed, dated it, and slid the whole thing back to her. She turned it over, checked the back, stamped it, and dropped it in a gray plastic bin with maybe thirty others.

"Everyone gets that wrong," she said. "First job?"

"First job."

She handed him an apron, folded into a neat square, and a rag. "There's a two-top by the window needs clearing, and the couple at six split a salad and neither one of them tipped. Welcome aboard."

He tied the apron. It was too long, and he doubled the strings at his back, and he picked up the gray bin of cleared plates with the rag thrown over his shoulder like something he'd seen in a movie, and crossed the dining room toward the window, where the light was starting to go amber over the parking lot.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: In The Two Fridas, one Frida wears a white European-style Victorian dress and the other wears a traditional Tehuana dress, a contrast often read as her mixed European and Mexican heritage.
story:
The portfolio deadline was Friday at three, and by Tuesday Ella had nine finished pieces and no statement, which meant she had no theme, only nine paintings that happened to live in the same folder. Ms. Okafor had been clear on the first day: ten artworks around one idea, plus a page of writing that explained why the idea was hers. The art room stayed open until five on Tuesdays, so Ella spread the nine across two tables and stood back with her arms crossed, trying to see what a stranger would see.

Dana and Marcus came in arguing, the way they usually did, carrying their own portfolios like luggage. They dropped into the stools at the next table and Dana slapped a printout of The Two Fridas between them, a reproduction small enough to lose the brushwork but big enough to show the double figure seated hand in hand, hearts exposed.

"The one in the Tehuana dress is the real Frida," Dana said. "The Mexican one. The other one's basically a costume."

"That's backwards," Marcus said. "The European dress is who she actually was half the time, married to Diego, living in that world. The white Victorian one. You can't just pick the dress you like better."

"The white one's the one with the cut heart, though," Dana said, tapping the figure on the left. "That's the one being abandoned."

"That doesn't make her more real. That makes her sadder."

Ella came over, mostly to stop the argument before it got loud enough to bring Ms. Okafor out of the kiln room. She looked at the printout for a long moment. "Maybe neither one's the costume," she said. "Maybe the whole point is that she's both, sitting there holding her own hand." Dana and Marcus both started talking at once, and Ella held up a palm. "I don't mean that as a compromise. I mean both dresses are hers. That's why there are two of her."

Marcus turned sardonic, the way he did when he thought someone was dodging. "So nothing's the real anything. Convenient."

"Fine, then the real one is the pair," Ella said. "One Frida in the Tehuana dress, one in the European one, and the real subject is the space between them." She was mostly saying it to end the argument, but the sentence kept going in her head after she stopped saying it out loud.

She walked back to her nine paintings and laid them out again in a different order. There was her grandmother's kitchen table with the plastic tablecloth; there was the school parking lot at dusk; there was the self-portrait she'd done holding her mother's rosary even though she didn't pray. She had been telling herself these were separate things, one for home and one for school, the way she was one person in Spanish at the dinner table and another in English in the hallway, and she had thought of that split as a problem the portfolio needed to route around. Dana and Marcus had wanted to know which Frida was real, and the painting refused to choose, and Ella understood suddenly that her folder had been refusing to choose all semester. Ten pieces about standing in two places at once, holding her own hand. It wasn't a dodge, or not only a dodge. It was a position, and positions could include a claim about what stayed uncertain. In her sketchbook she wrote a possible first line: I keep two dresses in the same closet, and the question of which one I really wear is the work.

She spent the last hour before five painting the tenth piece, small, on a scrap of good paper: two chairs at one table, one holding a plastic tablecloth, one holding a chemistry textbook, a single pair of hands in the middle shared between them. It was rough. It might reify the idea too neatly, pinning it like a butterfly before it had finished moving, and she noted in the margin to try it looser tomorrow. At five o'clock Ms. Okafor's keys jingled in the doorway and Dana leaned over Ella's table on her way out.

"That's your tenth?" Dana asked.

"That's my tenth."

Dana looked at it, then at the printout still lying facedown on the other table. "She should have painted them holding hands," she said, gathering her portfolio. "The two Fridas. Not just the one vein."

"She kind of did," Ella said, and turned off the light.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Papers posted on arXiv, the preprint server Paul Ginsparg started in 1991, are checked by moderators for relevance but are not peer reviewed before they appear.
story:
Peyton had claimed the table by the periodicals because it had the only outlet that worked, and because from there she could see the whole second floor, including the study room where her brother's science fair report was slowly killing him. Marcus was eleven, but he had the grim focus of a much older man. His poster board said WHAT REALLY KILLED THE DINOSAURS, and beneath the banner, in pencil, a sentence she could read from across the room.

She carried her coffee over and stood behind him. "Read that out loud," she said.

"Multiple studies confirm that the Chicxulub impact caused massive igneous activity that killed everything within weeks," Marcus read, chin up, like a lawyer resting his case.

"Multiple studies." She turned his laptop toward her. The source was a single paper, one, and when she scrolled to the top the orange banner of arXiv ran across the page like a hazard stripe. "Where'd you find this?"

"Devin's cousin. He's in grad school, so."

Peyton had been in exactly this chair, more or less, three years ago. She'd written a whole essay on volcanic deposits for Earth science, and her teacher, Ms. Okafor, had circled a citation and written "interesting, but check where this lives." Peyton had not checked, because checking felt like accusing herself, and the essay had gone up on the wall with an A-minus that she could still feel under her fingernails. When the class period ended and the posters came down, hers had gone into the recycling while she watched, and she'd felt a small private culpability, the kind nobody assigns detention for. She had exhumed the essay once, sophomore year, from an old folder, to see whether it was as bad as she remembered. It was worse. The paper she'd cited had never been published anywhere; it had just lived on the preprint server, waiting, patient as a fossil.

"Okay," she said, pulling out the chair across from him. "So, arXiv. You know what it is?"

"A website," Marcus said. "With science."

"It's a preprint server. This guy Paul Ginsparg started it in 1991." She tapped the banner. "Scientists put papers there before anyone's checked the actual science. There are moderators, but all they do is check that it's relevant, that it belongs on the site. It's not peer reviewed before it goes up."

Marcus looked at the screen like it had lied to him personally. "So it could be wrong."

"It could be wrong. It could also be right. That's the annoying part."

"Then why do they put it up?"

"Because other scientists read it and then try it themselves, and if it keeps working, and other people get the same result, then it starts to be something you can stand on." She slid the laptop back. "One paper is a guy at a party telling you something interesting. Ten papers is a conversation."

Marcus erased his sentence with the dedication of a man removing evidence. "So what do I write?"

"The truth. That one group found this, and other people are checking it, and that's how it works. Ms. Betancourt will like that better anyway. She told me last year she can always tell when somebody copied a claim." Peyton had learned that lesson late, in a recycling bin, but Marcus didn't need the whole autopsy.

He wrote for a while, tongue between his teeth. Peyton went back to her table and her own work, an application essay with the cursor blinking at her like a heartbeat monitor. Across the floor, two women by the microfilm machine were arguing in furious whispers about whether the machine still worked, which it did not; it had not worked since at least the Clinton administration, and every few months someone tried anyway, out of loyalty or spite.

Marcus reappeared at her shoulder twenty minutes later with the poster board under his arm. "I changed it. It says 'One study suggests, and other scientists are testing it.' And I cited it as a preprint." He said the last word carefully, newly owned. "Devin's cousin says that's the honest way."

"It is."

"Is my poster still good?"

"Better," she said. "Judges like a guy who knows what he doesn't know yet."

He considered this, then carried the poster down the stairs, holding it flat and level like something that could still spill. Peyton watched him go, then looked back at her essay, at the cursor, at the sentence she'd written about being certain of nothing except her willingness to find out. She deleted the whole sentence and started typing just as the microfilm machine, against all evidence, hummed to life behind her.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
story:
Julia had the whole Saturday planned down to the quarter hour, and the farmers' market was eating the plan alive. She had promised her mother a real dinner, a soup made from scratch, before her brother Marcus flew back to his second year of college on Sunday, and she had allotted exactly twenty minutes to buy onions, carrots, and a chicken from the Halloway farm stand. But Mrs. Halloway wanted to talk about Julia's upcoming departure too, and about her own daughter who had just started nursing school in Cleveland, and there was no polite way to hurry a woman handing you a free bag of carrot tops for stock.

"Your mother says you're doing the dinner tonight," Mrs. Halloway said, wrapping the chicken in butcher paper. "Marcus texted me about it. That boy valorizes your cooking like it's a religion, you know. Every time he comes home he tells me his sister makes better soup than anybody."

"He exaggerates," Julia said, though privately she held the opinion closer to fact than exaggeration. Tonight was supposed to prove something, though she would not have said what. That the kitchen could still be a place the family gathered, maybe, even after this year of dinners eaten in shifts. That she could leave for her dorm in two weeks having built something that would outlast her.

Marcus appeared at the mouth of the stand with a cup of cider and an expression of pure teenage grievance. "Mom says I have to help," he announced. "I'm being conscripted."

"You're being included," Julia said. She paid Mrs. Halloway, hefted the bag. "There's a difference. You can carry the onions."

At home the kitchen was warm and smelled faintly of the morning's coffee. Julia set out the cutting board and the three yellow onions from the bag, and she was circumspect about the knife, checking its edge against her thumbnail the way her father had taught her before he stopped cooking altogether. Marcus was assigned carrots and immediately began complaining about the peeler. Their mother drifted in and out, pretending to look for a ladle, plainly wanting to be asked to stay.

"You cry every time," Marcus said when the first onion was half chopped and Julia's eyes had begun to sting and stream. "It's an onion. Emotionally unstable behavior, honestly. Should we talk about your feelings?"

"It's not crying," Julia said, blinking hard, wiping her cheek with her wrist. "It's chemistry. Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, and that vapor irritates your eyes and makes them tear. It's a gas. It has nothing to do with my feelings."

"Syn-pro-what?"

"Propanethial-S-oxide. I read it. It's in the food science thing I've been looking at for school." She said it with more certainty than she felt. She had read it twice, actually, because the first time she had been half asleep, and she liked knowing the name of the thing that got her every single time. It was satisfying, in a way, to have an explanation that nobody could tease her about. Though she noticed Marcus chopping his own onion now, at the far end of the board, and his eyes were going red too.

"Okay," he admitted, sniffing. "That's real. Why does it feel like mace?"

"Because your eyes think it is," Julia said, and slid her board to the window ledge, where the breeze off the yard came through. That helped, somewhat. She went back to the pot, softening the onions in butter, and her mother finally sat down at the table with the peeler and a pile of carrots, taking over Marcus's abandoned post without being asked. Marcus leaned against the counter and told a story about his roommate, and the kitchen filled with the low heat of the onions going translucent, and Julia thought about how the cell walls were breaking down in the pan, the substrate of the whole soup turning sweet, everything sharp becoming something else.

"You know what I want," Marcus said suddenly, mid-story, apropos of nothing Julia could track. "When you're at school. Text me what you're making sometimes. Not a big thing. Just, like, Tuesday, you made soup. Because the food here is the only thing I actually miss."

"You miss Mom and Dad."

"I tolerate Mom and Dad. I miss the food." He grinned, but there was something careful underneath it, and Julia understood that he was asking for a thread, a small one, and that he had chosen this ridiculous way to ask because the plain way would have embarrassed them both.

She considered, while stirring, two ideas she had been carrying around all summer like coins in the same pocket. One was from her chemistry teacher, that everything worth knowing had a mechanism, a name, a reason the tears came. The other was older, from her grandmother, that you couldn't explain a good soup, you could only stand over it and pay attention. She had thought for a while that she would have to pick, that college meant choosing the explaining kind of life and letting the other one go. Standing at the stove with the market bag empty on the counter and her brother describing the vapor still stinging his eyes, she suspected they were not actually opposites. The gas had a name and the soup had a name and neither one was the whole of it, and she could not yet say how the two fit together, only that both had felt true in her hands today.

"I'll text you," she said. "Tuesdays and Sundays. Soup report." She dipped the wooden spoon, blew on it, and held it out across the stove for Marcus to taste. "Careful. It's hot."
